A Space Probe Returns to Asteroids Where NASA Tested Planetary Defense Systems

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage.
  • Sources indicate that astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth.
  • In the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage. We don't have to look all that far back for an example. In 1908, in an incident now known as the “Tunguska Event,” a space rock, likely a few dozen meters wide, exploded over Siberia. Though scientists weren’t able to visit the site for another two decades, the landscape was still scarred from the explosion.

Sources indicate that astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth. The 450-meter-wide body will miss us at a distance of only 19,000 miles. That’s about 12 times closer to us than the moon and much closer than many satellites. It will even be visible to the naked eye.

In the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions. As space probes deepen our knowledge of small bodies in the solar system, astronomers have increasingly reliable and detailed data for finding potentially hazardous asteroids. Our ability to respond to such a threat, however, is another story. This is the missing and extremely important link—planetary defense technology that could allow us to deflect a dangerous object in time.

It has been revealed that in a sci-fi flick, such situations are often solved with a nuclear bomb. But in the real world, blowing up a big space rock into tiny bits is not ideal. Instead, it’s better to alter the asteroid's orbit. Everything in the vacuum of space is in motion. Our own planet travels about 20 miles every second. If the object hurtling towards us can be slowed down and thus reach the meeting point a little later, it will simply miss the Earth.

According to recent reports, four years ago, this was essentially what NASA tested on a pair of celestial bodies known as Didymos and Dimorphos. Astronomers at the Kitt Peak Observatory discovered Didymos, an asteroid measuring 780 meters across, 30 years ago. A few years later, Czech astronomer Petr Pravec observed that this asteroid had a “moonlet” orbiting it about every 12 hours. This smaller body, measuring about 151 meters in diameter, was then named Dimorphos.

The paired objects were a perfect testing ground for the kind of deflection a planetary defense system would involve. Locked in on these targets, NASA rolled out the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) in late 2021. Nearly a year later, the DART probe crashed into Dimorphos.

Sources indicate that scientists had hoped that the impact of the probe—which was barreling toward the asteroids at over 13,000 miles per hour—could shorten the period of the mini-moon's orbit by a minute or more. In the end, it was slowed down by 33 minutes. This major deviation was caused by the ejection of debris, leading to a much greater recoil than what was produced by the impact itself. In addition, the orbital speed of both asteroids around the sun also slowed. And in a sense, Dimorphos briefly became a comet—the debris released by the impact creating a long tail behind it.

But questions remain about the longer-term impacts of this test. In October 2024, the European Space Agency (ESA) sent off the space probe Hera to rendezvous with both asteroids. After a flyby of Mars, the probe began its arrival phase this past October. It took its first image about 800 miles away, and the first detailed image of Didymos was published in early November.

Sources indicate that now in their vicinity, Hera will study both bodies in depth. Though there’s much we can learn about asteroids by observing them from our planet, nothing can replace close-up exploration, and this will be the first time a binary asteroid system will be explored in detail. One of the mission's goals is to find out how such asteroid pairs form. Didymos is also interesting for its rapid rotation, turning once every 2.3 hours—placing it on the very edge of stability.

It has been revealed that but of course, beyond this traditional astronomy research, which could also take place at another set of binary asteroids, Hera will investigate the consequences of the DART mission. This will include studying the impact site. Because there are so many knowns about the impact itself, scientists can also use this opportunity to understand craters more broadly, answering questions such as whether the strength of the material or gravity plays a more decisive role in crater formation.

It has been revealed that hera will also determine the exact mass of Dimorphos, an important detail in assessing the effectiveness of the DART mission as a test of planetary defense technology. The probe also contains a lidar instrument for mapping the asteroid's topography and instruments for investigating the chemical composition of the surface. Additionally, we can expect to see detailed images of the asteroids taken with a resolution of 1 meter per pixel.

In a recent development, the probe is also carrying two miniature, cube-shaped satellites, called “CubeSats” for short, which it will deploy in January 2027. In Earth’s orbit, CubeSats are often used for simple experiments, including student projects, and they can even be stacked together to create larger satellites.

In a recent development, hera’s CubeSats, named Juventas and Milani, will attempt to land on the surface. Using radar capable of probing up to a depth of 100 meters, Juventas will focus on geophysical exploration of the asteroid Dimorphos. Additionally, a gravimeter on board will measure how the gravity on Dimorphos changes during its orbit due to the parent asteroid, Didymos. Meanwhile, Milani will carry out a detailed investigation of the asteroids’ surface composition and will search for traces of dust and the volatile substances contained within many space rocks.

In a recent development, according to current plans, this main phase of the Hera probe's mission is expected to last until the summer of next year, and findings from this probe will likely only become more relevant, not just as Apophis approaches, but even after it slings back into space. In the year 2000, we knew of only 300 near-Earth asteroids—those that approach Earth or directly cross its orbit. Today, we know of over 43,000.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Al-Qadisiyah University’s move a sign of the country’s slide into a Taliban-like gender segregation, say activists.

The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.

As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.

The university said the move was necessary to “prevent the mixing” of men and women and had been requested by the families of female students. But students said their families had known since before they enrolled that there were men on the teaching staff and supported their daughters’ protest.

Students said university bosses had mocked their protests and refused to discuss their concerns about the sudden loss of their academic supervisors. On social media, commentators also accused the women of seeking to keep male professors to “establish immoral relationships with them”.

Recent findings suggest that “My classmates and I went to demonstrate, and the university president, Rahi al-Yasiri, blocked our path with his bodyguards, who then began making fun of us. He ordered them to take photographs of our faces, in an attempt to intimidate us and punish us later,” said Huda, 22, one of the female students.

It has been revealed that huda mentioned the students tried to explain how men and women still worked together in society in Iraq. “Aren’t there doctors who treat both men and women? Why then do you prevent male professors from teaching us, too?” In response, Huda said Al-Yasiri replied: “Even if you hit your heads against the wall, I will not bring back the professors.”.

Recent findings suggest that the students mentioned a large number of them were tied to graduation projects and research supervised by the professors. They said they had grown accustomed to their professors’ teaching methods, who also knew their students’ strengths and weaknesses, which made replacing them at this stage more complicated.

Female students remarked they had been told by the university that if they were not happy with the change, they should drop out.

An Iraqi-British feminist researcher, Balsam Mustafa, from the University of Cardiff, noted the female students were “treated as if they are minors without the right to object to decisions affecting their academic lives”.

Mustafa stated the removal of the male professors was a part of a worrying trend in women’s rights in the country, with “growing discussion about women’s clothing and chastity reflected in the celebration of female students who wear the abaya”.

An Iraqi lawyer and human rights activist, Israa Salman, remarked the restrictions on women was a “societal catastrophe”.

“Attempts are being made to suppress women’s talents and turn Iraqi society – a society that has produced remarkable minds and expertise, with women playing pioneering roles in many fields – into something resembling Kabul under Taliban rule.

“This contradicts Iraq’s constitution and the international treaties and conventions the country has signed and ratified,” said Salman.

Convicted former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest over a coup attempt, has been hospitalized with abdominal pain.

Bolsonaro's son Carlos wrote on X that the former far-right leader was taken to the hospital on Friday and was found to have "a near-complete intestinal obstruction.".

The DF Star Hospital in Brasília mentioned that Bolsonaro was suffering from "abdominal distension" and was being examined.

​Bolsonaro, who is 71 years old, ‌has undergone several hospitalizations and surgeries since he was stabbed in the abdomen on the campaign trail for the 2018 elections.

"He is being given medication for pain and an initial attempt to reverse the condition without the need for invasive intervention," Carlos noted.

Bolsonaro was in power from 2019 to ​2022. He was convicted last year for plotting a coup after his defeat to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the 2022 election but claims being the victim of a left-wing judicial witch hunt.

Bolsonaro was placed under humanitarian house arrest on medical grounds.

Carlos on Friday railed against his father's detention, which he blamed for Bolsonaro's current health problems.

Carlos stated that the senior Bolsonaro's health was "deteriorating every day in prison due to his lack of mobility" and what he called "the psychological torture he suffers daily.".

Another one of Bolsonaro's sons, Flavio Bolsonaro, recently lost the October presidential election to incumbent President Lula. Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil after the vote and now resides in Florida.

'I tell my son it's just fireworks': Life inside Yemeni city besieged by Houthis

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1864 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say.
  • In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
  • Sources indicate that "When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she claims.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say.

In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

Sources indicate that "When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she claims. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life.".

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

It has been revealed that they gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city.

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.

From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.

In a recent development, estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

According to recent reports, some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.

Industry observers note that "Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," indicates Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

"It used to be a lively city," she states. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous.".

She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.

"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she indicates.

Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade.

War is not fresh to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.

Recent findings suggest that houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

Recent findings suggest that more than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.

A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.

In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.

An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.

Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he indicates. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him.".

It has been revealed that most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.

According to recent reports, they arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", claims Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.

He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".

Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor says.

If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.

"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," notes Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.

It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.

Sources indicate that "The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he states. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents.".

We have not been able to independently verify these figures.

Sources indicate that he remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.

On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.

Industry observers note that the Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.

That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.

What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.

He states the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

Industry observers note that "Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".

Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.

How long can the city hold out, I ask.

"Until the population perishes," he replies.

Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.

They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.

Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.

Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.

Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (Â£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.

He tells us this fight is different to 2015.

"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he notes. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves.".

He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.

It has been revealed that but Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He indicates that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".

The armed group is presently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the glitch) but not by the UK or the European Union.

It has been revealed that "They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," states Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city.".

Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months.

But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.

According to recent reports, "Every night we have bombing and shelling," indicates Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes.".

In a recent development, the people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he claims, "because we don't see any move to help us.".

Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.

But could they fight their way in?

Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.

"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he indicates.

His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.

Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.

"I tell them it's a party," he notes, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a major party.".

As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.

"Please don't forget Taiz," she notes. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports.".

Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor.

#82133. Industry News: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1289 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
  • The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used.
  • Recent findings suggest that the updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

Recent findings suggest that the updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a upcoming research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

In a recent development, and AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the organization (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

It has been revealed that though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” states Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”.

Industry observers note that kapoor claims he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor states. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR's research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” notes Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”.

In a recent development, matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, indicates that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”.

In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In the newly introduced report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how promptly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet.
  • Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.
  • Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet.

Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.

“So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” notes Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.

Mykola operates a marshrutka, a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.

Passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.

“It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.

Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.

In a recent development, moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

Recent findings suggest that as of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The latest Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.

Sources indicate that the Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.

In a recent development, dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, noted it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.

Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch.

Yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he said, behind Istanbul and Moscow.

Particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov remarked – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.

At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” stated Nataliya, a customer service specialist.

Recent findings suggest that iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something newly introduced.”.

Recent findings suggest that it is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy.

Oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he stated.

Additional reporting by Galya Rudyk.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement’s midterm wipeout, a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But a Stat report on MAHA’s own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group’s priority was ever winning elections in the first place.

The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates.

Recent findings suggest that the findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA’s clout in the midterms. In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously.

According to Stat’s findings, of the $10.5 million the MAHA PAC spent on the midterms, less than a tenth—roughly $1 million—went to messaging on political candidates, which are expenses called “independent expenditures.”.

Andrew Mayersohn, a committees researcher at OpenSecrets, called the spending “pretty unusual,” explaining that “Major super PACs spend most of their money on independent expenditures.”.

Recent findings suggest that in some cases, the scant political spending was dwarfed by spending on luxuries. For instance, in a key House race in Northern California, MAHA supported Kevin Kiley over his political rival, pediatrician Richard Pan. Despite calling the race “the most direct ideological confrontation” between MAHA and its opposition “anywhere on the 2026 ballot,” the PAC only spent $49,900 to back Kiley. That’s a little less than the $50,100 it spent at Mastro’s Steakhouse, an upscale restaurant that offers $110 porterhouse steaks in Washington, DC. Further, it’s less than a third of the $155,900 the PAC spent at Ned’s Club, a luxury club near the White House that has become a popular gathering spot among Trump officials.

Kiley lost the election to Pan by double digits.

Industry observers note that of the roughly $1 million spent on political candidates, most of it—over $700,000—went to defeating Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.). Many other MAHA-endorsed candidates received $50,000 or less. Some got less than $2,000.

It has been revealed that outside of steaks and a private club, the MAHA PAC spent $500,000 on a media firm, Merit Street Media, run by Phil McGraw, who hosted a MAHA special featuring Dr. Phil. MAHA leaders used PAC money to cover meals, payroll, and credit card bills. The PAC paid $275,000 to a security firm, Gavin de Becker & Associates, which is led by an ally of anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., MAHA’s top leader. Tens of thousands more went to LLCs that have little to no online information.

According to recent reports, on the other hand, prominent online MAHA influencers also pocketed tens of thousands from the PAC, as did writers for The MAHA Report, a Substack that promotes Kennedy and MAHA interests. In the days after the midterms, as members of the movement were coming to grips with the election losses, The MAHA Report chose to publish a lengthy article defending convicted rapist Russel Brand, a Kennedy ally who became a MAHA fixture.

In a recent development, the biggest chunk of the MAHA PAC’s spending—more than $3 million—went to the nonprofit MAHA Action, which is also run by Lyons. It’s unclear how all that money was spent.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit.

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's fresh political generation and its giant neighbour.

It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.

The talks are expected to cover a broad range of complications, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of latest air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.

The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.

India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).

Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.

Nepal suffered devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,450 people and left thousands missing.

But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Substantial Brother' attitude of Delhi.

Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.

"The new Nepali leadership states they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.

It has been revealed that "They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.

Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.

Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them â the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN â UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).

Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.

Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.

But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.

The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.

Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.

India and Nepal share an open border and longstanding economic ties.

It has been revealed that one key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.

Industry observers note that "India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.

India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.

Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.

In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.

The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.

"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.

Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its latest airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.

Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.

Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.

Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.

Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.

His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.

But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.

"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," indicates Dixit.

Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.

Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.

Industry observers note that while Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

Three Salvadoran soldiers were killed in Haiti while handling explosives, El Salvador's military said on Friday.

The incident marks the first officially reported deaths since a 2,000-member Salvadoran military contingent was deployed to the gang violence-stricken Caribbean nation last month.

One of the soldiers succumbed to his injuries while being treated in the neighboring Dominican Republic, where he was airlifted to, the El Salvador military noted on X.

Another soldier was wounded in the incident and is out of danger, it added.

It was not immediately clear where the blast took place.

The Salvadoran military's statement also did not give any further details on the type of explosives the soldiers were working with.

"We extend our deepest condolences and solidarity to the families of the three deceased," it mentioned.

Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele sent over 2,000 troops and special forces to Haiti to rescue four El Salvador airmen — members of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF)—  who went missing after a gang ambush on October 18 in the Haitian capital of Port-au-Prince.

The additional troops dispatched by Bukele are not part of the GSF, and the contingent's remit appears to have broadened to stamp out Haitian gangs.

Bukele, who has been known for his tough approach to the gangs in El Salvador, has posted several videos of strikes on residences of gang leaders around Port-au-Prince.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Meanwhile, on Friday, Haiti confirmed an agreement with El Salvador to build three fresh Haitian prisons.

The development follows this week's visit to El Salvador by Haiti's security and justice minister, Patrick Pelissier.

The prisons will be built by a Salvadoran company in collaboration with a Haitian firm, Pelissier stated.

Sources indicate that haitian prisons are notoriously overcrowded. In 2024, gang raids in two of the country's biggest penitentiaries saw thousands of inmates being released.

El Salvador, on the other hand, is home to a notorious maximum security mega-prison known as Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT).

The country has imprisoned over 90,000 people with no access to family visits ever since entering a state of exception in 2022.

Pelissier visited CECOT during his trip to El Salvador.

"Once you enter, there is no hope of ever seeing the outside world again," the Haitian minister mentioned as he praised the mega-prison.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I hate running out of power.
  • Most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options.
  • Updated November 2026: I added power banks from Anker, Peak Design, Nitecore, and Iniu, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I hate running out of power. Everybody does. While our gadgets have advanced in many ways, battery technology has been slow to improve. That’s why you’re looking to buy a power bank. A good portable charger is a handy backup that can keep your smartphone, tablet, and maybe even your laptop going for longer. I’ve been testing power banks for years. I’ve tested more than 100 portable chargers. But you only really need one or two.

Most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options. Read the Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks for more magnetic wireless chargers, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations for more power.

Updated November 2026: I added power banks from Anker, Peak Design, Nitecore, and Iniu, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.

Sources indicate that this is the only power bank you need. Anker combines style and substance with this versatile power bank that packs a whopping 25,000-mAh capacity and is capable of delivering up to 165 watts to two devices (100 watts for a single device connected via USB-C). I love the rounded edges, the retractable, flat 2.3-foot USB-C cable up top, and the clever braided 1-foot USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop. It has a display to show the remaining battery, charging rate in and out, battery temperature, and health. It supports pass-through charging and takes around two hours to recharge.

OK, you don’t really need this many stats, but having a precise idea of how much power remains is useful and reassuring. I love the built-in cables, because they ensure you’re never caught without one. This is also below the limit for power banks on flights, so you can travel with it. Anker’s Laptop Power Bank fast-charged everything I tested it with, including multiple smartphones, an iPad, a Poco tablet, a MacBook Air, and a Chromebook. You can charge four devices simultaneously without any issues. After a year of use, mine still performs perfectly.

You don’t always need significant capacity, and you don’t always have room for a big power bank. If you want something more portable, go for the Nimble Champ Pro. At 6.2 ounces, it’s one of the lightest on the market. It’s smaller than a deck of cards and can deliver 20 watts to charge two devices at once via a USB-C port on either end. It feels durable, comes in a snazzy new range of speckled color finishes, and has a bright lanyard loop that makes for easy carrying and helps you pick it out of your backpack. The Pro version is bigger but doubles the capacity (to 20,000 mAh) and has a similar design with two USB-C ports that go up to 65 watts. There’s also a smaller version with a 5,200-mAh capacity that tops out at 15 watts.

Recent findings suggest that another reason I like Nimble is its environmental efforts. Batteries are not environmentally benign. They use lithium, cobalt, and other rare metals whose supply chains are environmentally and socially questionable at best. But Nimble’s use of bioplastics and plastic-free minimal packaging at least reduces the environmental impact where it can be reduced. This version uses 90 percent recycled plastic (up 25 percent from the original) and comes in smaller plastic-free packaging. Nimble includes a 3.3-foot USB-C to USB-C cable in the box.

The original was the first Qi2 power bank I tested and was my top pick for quite a while, but this sequel is even better. The Qi2 wireless charging standard borrows elements of Apple’s MagSafe, enabling supported phones to connect with perfect alignment using a ring of magnets. Because it works with Apple's StandBy mode, you can stick Qi2 or MagSafe phones in portrait or landscape orientation.

In a recent development, qi2 brings faster wireless charging rates of up to 25 watts, but it is also backward compatible, so older Qi devices can still charge (albeit more slowly). This compact portable charger has a handy kickstand, a two-way USB-C port on the left edge, and a power button with an LED display that can show remaining power as a percentage. It can also display charging time when plugged in, watts out, temperature, and battery health. Anker offers the device in a range of fun colors (I love the burgundy). What Features Should I Look for in Power Banks?

There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.

In a recent development, the capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get depends on the cable you use, the device you’re charging, and the charging method. (Qi wireless charging is less efficient.) You will never get the maximum capacity from any power bank. You can generally expect to get between 60 and 80 percent after energy loss through heat and conversion. Some manufacturers list a “Rated Capacity” that’s lower than the overall capacity to give you an indication of what to expect in real-world use. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for devices.

The charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. Many smartphones, including Apple’s iPhones, support the power delivery standard, meaning you can use higher-power power banks to recharge the device with no issues. A few phones, such as Samsung’s Galaxy S range, support a supplementary PD protocol called PPS (programmable power supply) that goes up to 45 watts. Many phones also support Qualcomm’s proprietary Quick Charge (QC) standard. There are also other proprietary fast-charging standards, but you won’t generally find power banks that support them unless they come from the smartphone manufacturer.

Your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. The Nimble, GoalZero, Biolite, Mophie, Zendure, and Sharge portable chargers listed support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. Monoprice does not support pass-through charging either. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.

Can I Take a Power Bank on a Plane?

It’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours. If your power bank has a larger capacity than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.

According to recent reports, some airlines introduced stricter rules in 2025, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have on board.

Why You Should Avoid Cheap Power Banks.

Many years ago, the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 gained notoriety when its batteries caught fire in a series of incidents. There’s been a steady stream of similar, though isolated, incidents ever since. Despite the high-profile coverage of batteries gone wrong, the vast majority of lithium-ion batteries are safe.

Industry observers note that the chemical reaction that occurs inside a lithium-ion cell is complex, but as in any battery, there’s a negative and a positive electrode. In lithium batteries, the negative is a lithium-carbon compound, and the positive is cobalt oxide (though many battery makers are moving away from cobalt). These two compounds cause a reaction that is safe when controlled and delivers energy to your devices. When the reaction gets out of control, though, you end up with earbuds melting in your ears. What changes a safe reaction to an uncontrolled reaction can be any number of things: excess heat, physical damage during use, physical damage during manufacture, or using the wrong charger.

The three basic rules that have kept me safe through testing dozens and dozens of batteries are these:.

Avoiding cheap wall-outlet adapters, cords, and chargers is the most important rule. These are your most likely sources of problems. Those chargers you see on Amazon for $20 cheaper than the competition? Not worth it. They probably got the price down by skimping on insulation, leaving out power-management tools, and ignoring the basics of electrical safety. Price alone is no guarantee of safety, either. Buy from reputable companies and brands.

According to recent reports, then there’s heat. Too much of it can cause all manner of problems, both in terms of discharge and safety. Avoid heat, and pay attention to your batteries when they’re charging. If your device gets overly hot when charging, this can be a sign of problems. Similarly, beware of any swollen, bulging, or otherwise misshapen batteries.

Why Is My Power Bank Charging Slowly?

I’ve explained charging rates and capacity above, but several factors can cause charging speed to be slower than expected. The rate is determined by the device being charged, so your phone will request a certain wattage, which changes depending on how full its battery is, on-device settings, and the battery temperature.

Industry observers note that all devices charge more slowly when they are completely empty, when the battery approaches full, and when they overheat. The cable you use will also have a maximum charging rate, and so will different ports on the power bank. Wireless charging is more convenient, but also slower than wired charging.

I’ve been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test phone (at the moment an iPhone 16). I’ll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S24+ to test charging speeds, and whatever else I have in. For larger-capacity power banks, I test-charge an iPad Mini and a MacBook Air. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.

Aside from these standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it’s not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.

How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?

According to recent reports, I often scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown upcoming brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to those companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would go against WIRED’s editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision on ranking.

Recent findings suggest that there are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to known, reputable brands, but there’s always room for something latest if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.
  • I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website.
  • According to recent reports, amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.

I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged in to Amazon.

According to recent reports, amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.

Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:.

Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in Newly introduced York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.

It’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April. What is upcoming is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.

Industry observers note that the messaging suggests that Amazon is concerned about the potential impact the proposed law would have on its costs. Besides Amazon, the bill targets any company with last-mile delivery facilities in NYC, like FedEx and DoorDash.

According to recent reports, it also raises questions about the potential impact on shoppers should Amazon expand its use of its e-commerce platform for additional political messaging. The pop-up launched today impacts only NYC residents but sets a precedent for Amazon to sway political views on other issues. Amazon has made similar moves internally, including reportedly using an app for its employees to campaign against unionizing. But the fresh pop-up shows Amazon extending that strategy directly to its consumers.

Given Amazon’s considerable influence in commerce, other companies could copy its actions. Uber and Lyft have previously done so, CNBC reports.

Recent findings suggest that finally, there’s the question of whether Amazon is fairly depicting the situations surrounding the bill. Notable supporters of the Delivery Protection Act include NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Using a platform with massive reach to communicate only one side of an ongoing debate could lead to misinformation and a skewed public perception.

According to recent reports, the Delivery Protection Act is at the moment stalled in the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. The last hearing on the bill was in April. A committee vote on whether to advance the act to the full City Council hasn’t been set.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All options open in future talks, notes Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’.

The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said.

The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday.

In a recent development, agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme were revealed after talks this week. Under the intends, 100,000 young Britons will be allowed to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with similar access for Europeans in the UK.

Burnham said the agreement would add 0.5% to the UK’s GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.

In a recent development, miliband noted Burnham would have further “brainstorming” discussions with the EU in the next year about what could happen next. He said the agreements this week were the limit of what could be done before the next general election.

However, the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.

Miliband said in an interview for the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that “all the options will be on the table” when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding: “We will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options.”.

Industry observers note that since entering government in 2024, Labour has stuck to the “red lines” in its manifesto, which stated the party would not rejoin the single market or customs union. It also ruled out freedom of movement.

Burnham has previously noted he wants to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime.

The prime minister will use the announcement of his 10-year blueprint before Christmas to explore how the UK could get closer to the EU after the next election. Informal discussions will take place with Brussels before next year’s UK-EU summit.

Miliband said he accepts the result of the 2016 vote but “the world has changed massively”.

It has been revealed that “Europe is changing too, so we’ve got to look at what that means,” he stated. “It’s not about this parliament, we’re respecting the red lines in this parliament.”.

He also denied the deal with the EU would rely on progress in discussions on students from the bloc coming to the UK. It has been reported that a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

Miliband told the BBC it was “absolutely clear” the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

The foreign secretary remarked: “The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we’re introducing legislation in parliament, so definitely.”.

Recent findings suggest that on Friday, Burnham noted the agreement represented a “good day for Britain and Europe”. He said the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.

“The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” Burnham mentioned, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”. About the further discussions, she noted: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”.

Recent findings suggest that the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday the deal was good for farmers. “(It) will open up new markets. They’ll be able to import and expor. This is a win-win for the UK. We will dissolve a lot of the friction and costs at the border for UK agriculture and food.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You can also easily add other users to your HomeView display.

Recent findings suggest that apple HomeView has arrived, and to set up the smart display, you'll have to use your iPhone or iPad. Unlike other companies' smart displays, the HomeView doesn't run its own apps; it merely mirrors the compatible ones you have on your phone or tablet. It's similar to CarPlay in that regard.

In a recent development, some of those apps are part of Apple's own core suite, including Calendar, Messages, Reminders and Weather. However, the HomeView will not actually host or have access to your personal information. It will only show things like texts and calendar reminders if it can verify your identity through your face and if your paired iPhone or iPad is nearby. The idea is for all members of your household to be able to use the HomeView without compromising anybody's privacy.

It has been revealed that the good news is that pairing it with an iPhone or an iPad is fairly easy. To start with, your iPhone must be running the recently released iOS 27.2, while your iPad must be running iPadOS 27.2. In addition, to be able to make the most of HomeView, you'll have to be comfortable running Apple Intelligence. It's always listening to your Siri queries, and you'll need to use Siri AI, the next-generation version of the assistant powered by Apple Intelligence, to get more useful and conversational responses.

It has been revealed that the process of pairing and iPhone or iPad to a HomeView device is simple. You just have to hold your phone or tablet near the smart display that's powered on. You'll then see a card pop up, similar to a upcoming set of AirPods or other Apple devices. If you're not running the latest iOS or iPadOS software, you'll be prompted to patch. Follow the on-screen directions (more on those below) and you're good to go.

If you don't see a card, or if you close it accidentally, there is a more manual setup method for the HomeView. After you revision your operating system, open the Home app on your phone or tablet. If you've never used it before, you have to set up a new Home. Tap the + icon at the top-right corner of the screen, then Add New Home and give it a name. You will automatically be listed as the Home's Resident (Owner). If you already have a Home set up, tap the ellipsis icon at the top right, choose a Home and make sure you're its Resident (Owner).

Next, open the Find My app and then make sure Shared From is set to This iPhone or This iPad. If it's not set to that option, and you see Use This [device] as My Location, tap it. Check that your phone's Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are switched on. If you haven't powered on your HomeView yet, do it now. Unlock your iPhone or iPad and place it near the HomeView to see a Set Up screen appear on your device.

Now, it's time to pair your devices. You'll see a prompt on your iPhone or iPad, asking you to Center HomeView in the camera frame to capture the animation on the bigger screen. You can also tap on Enter Passcode Manually to get HomeView to show you a four-digit passcode instead. After the frame in the setup screen turns green, the process begins.

Recent findings suggest that you will be asked which Home to add the HomeView to. After you've chosen, you'll get to the Where will you use this HomeView screen, where you'll have to choose the room where you want to add it to. Take note that you may be asked to update the HomeView software. After the update is done, you'll go through more prompts, including one that asks if you want your HomeView to match your iPhone settings, like your Wi-Fi network and Siri voice. Another prompt asks if you want the HomeView to be able to show personal content like messages. Once you're done, the display will show an animation while it's undergoing configuration.

From here, the setup process will move to the HomeView itself. You'll be asked to set up Face and Voice Recognition for a more personalized experience. Remember that you can't display messages and other personal information on the HomeView without authenticating your identity. Tap Continue and follow the instructions.

It has been revealed that to set up Voice Recognition, you'll have to read several prompts shown on screen out loud. Next, you'll be able to set Facial Recognition by positioning your face in the center of the camera frame and moving it, according to the instructions on screen. This process is similar to setting up Face ID on other Apple devices. The HomeView will then show you a short tutorial of its features. The moment the Welcome screen appears, you know you're done.

Sources indicate that apple's HomeView supports up to six users on a single device, and you — or the user listed as Resident (Owner) of the Home it has been linked to — can add them after setup is done. Open the Home app and choose the Home linked to your device. Tap the + icon and choose Add People. When asked to choose their Role, choose Resident so they can access the HomeView anytime. You will then be asked to enter their Apple/iCloud account contact and then send them an invite. They can accept the invitation in the More section that shows up when you tap the ellipsis icon at the top right corner of the Home app.

According to recent reports, after a user has been added, they can swipe up on the HomeView to access the Home Screen and then tap the profile icon at the top right to choose their account. Once the user brings their iPhone or iPad near the HomeView, a prompt with a Join button appear on their device. They will also have to go through several prompts, including the one asking them if they want the display to match their iPhone settings and whether they want it to show any personal information. They will then officially be added as a user and will be able to set up Voice and Facial Recognition. One user only has to swipe down the Home Screen to exit, and another user can take over once they step in front of the HomeView.

These dead pets were meant to be cremated - then their bodies appeared on a livestream
