  • A man â bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses â walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.
  • Names are written on the packages â Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet â and numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revecca Calling is devastated after hearing about the bodies that were found and wants to know if her dog, Olaf, really was cremated.

A man â bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses â walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages â Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet â and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.

Recent findings suggest that it's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs.".

"Purebreds," says the woman filming.

Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting.

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In a recent development, in total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.

Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

In a recent development, now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.

One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.

A string of grisly discoveries in the suburbs near Manila has put thousands of grieving pet owners on edge.

When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.

It has been revealed that chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.

It has been revealed that on 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.

According to recent reports, chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting â taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.

"I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know.".

Recent findings suggest that in the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.

Industry observers note that "The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.

"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.

Chris Taylor, pictured here with a dog unrelated to the scandal, has uncovered the remains of some 170 dead pets in recent weeks.

By crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals. "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris states. "Others were liquefied.".

LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.

Recent findings suggest that their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.

Some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.

There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?

As more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.

"So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," says Chris. "And man, it just flooded in.".

Ahjay Paws, the company that was supposed to cremate Olaf, is under investigation.

The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.

It has been revealed that A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.

As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.

"Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a significant thing with the boom of the pet industry," notes Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets.".

These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.

Pet care - including for those that have died - has become a booming industry in the Philippines.

Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, claims she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (Â£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.

Calling claims Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.

When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated.

According to recent reports, "Pet owners entrust these services with something very crucial: the remains of a beloved family member," she notes. "We need to know what happened.".

Pets have been found dumped in bags like this - with labels giving their names and weights.

Earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.

According to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT â but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.

One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.

But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.

There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law â estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them â and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.

Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The company is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.

The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm said the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".

The pet-dumping scandal, in which Olaf may have been a victim, has blown up into a national controversy.

Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, says she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (Â£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago.

Industry observers note that "I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she says. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his.".

Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns.".

Sources indicate that in response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.

Industry observers note that the animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.

On 2 November, Percival Vilar CendaÃ±a of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace.

In a recent development, "Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations.".

In a recent development, neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real â and CendaÃ±a was giving voice to a common sentiment.

"Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he said.

At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.

But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.

Industry observers note that cabrera states the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".

It has been revealed that the scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like CendaÃ±a are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.

Meanwhile, Cabrera claims Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.

Chris Taylor dealing with items resembling clothing found at a dumpsite (blurred at source).

One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak".

"I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she remarked.

Chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he says.

It has been revealed that "They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them.".

It has been revealed that as well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he indicates.

Recent findings suggest that the BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr stated authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN.

"Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez noted.

"To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families.".

Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.

On Monday, the National Police Commission declared an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.

Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more.

"We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," notes Calling.â¯ "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever.".

According to recent reports, legada, for her part, notes: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated.".

She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days.".

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • According to recent reports, the Apple Watch has become a must-have device for many people, and it can last for years.
    • According to recent reports, that might make you wonder what you should do with an old, discontinued Apple Watch that you no longer use.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Your old Apple Watch might still be worth some cash when you trade it in for a latest one.

    According to recent reports, the Apple Watch has become a must-have device for many people, and it can last for years. Chances are that you'll probably buy a upcoming watch before your current one stops working. Still, your old Apple Watch will eventually stop getting software updates — that's what happened this year with watchOS 27, which dropped support for models older than the Series 9. Some of them still get security patches, but the latest features are exclusive to newer devices.

    According to recent reports, that might make you wonder what you should do with an old, discontinued Apple Watch that you no longer use. Even if you have a legacy Apple Watch, you can resell it or use it for trade-in credit at Apple. They aren't worth much, but it's better than leaving them unused in a drawer to gather dust.

    Industry observers note that if you don't want to deal with the hassle of selling your old Apple Watch on your own, the Apple Trade In program is the easiest path. With this, you give your used Apple Watch to Apple and you get credit toward a new product in return — that could be another Apple Watch or anything else, like AirPods or even an iPhone.

    Recent findings suggest that apple regularly updates its trade-in pricing table; at the time of writing, you can get as much as $430 in credit for an Apple Watch. The credit amount depends on the model you have and its condition, like whether it's in good shape or has scratches and cracks. If your Apple Watch is an especially old model or badly damaged, Apple won't offer trade-in credit for it, but it still offers free recycling.

    Trade-in values start at up to $30 for the first-generation Apple Watch SE, which came out in 2020. An Apple Watch Series 8 is worth $90 max, while a Series 11 is worth up to $200. The Ultra offers the highest trade-in value: Apple pays up to $430 for a used Apple Watch Ultra 3 in good condition. So for example, if you have a Series 8 in good condition and trade it in for a fresh Apple Watch Series 12 (which starts at $399), the price drops to $309 instead.

    Keep in mind that Apple doesn't pay cash for trade-in products. If you don't strategy on buying a upcoming product right away, or want the credit for something else, you can receive the value as an Apple gift card instead. It's thus a good way to cover the cost of apps or subscriptions.

    Sources indicate that you can bring your old watch to an Apple Store or mail it in — all shipping costs are covered. Apple adds your trade-in credit to your account balance as soon as it receives your watch and confirms that everything is in order.

    Selling an old Apple Watch on your own takes more effort, but also pays you more. On Swappa, a marketplace for used tech, a Series 6 can be worth around $100 — more than double the $45 Apple offers for it. The same applies to other models, like the Series 8, which is worth around $130.

    It has been revealed that the amount you can get will depend on which device you have and its condition. Apple Watch models with cellular connectivity and more premium materials, such as steel or titanium, tend to hold their value better than GPS-only and aluminum ones. Just remember to unpair and reset your Apple Watch before trading it in or selling it. Otherwise, Activation Lock will remain enabled, and the buyer won't be able to unlock it without your Apple Account and password. Apple refuses devices with Activation Lock enabled.

    And if you decide to keep your old Apple Watch after all, there are some interesting ways to put an older smartwatch to good use, like turning it into your sleep tracker while your main watch charges overnight.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Moscow intelligence thought to be behind initiative to kill musician Kyivstoner before concert in Denmark.
    • Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper.
    • “We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,” Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Moscow intelligence thought to be behind initiative to kill musician Kyivstoner before concert in Denmark.

    Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper.

    “We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,” Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. The expulsion will happen within seven days.

    “We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” he added.

    Danish police stated they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services ⁠to kill the US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in September before a planned performance in Denmark.

    Industry observers note that rasmussen also noted that Denmark was considering suspending Schengen visas to Russians. “We have launched work at the European level to further tighten the rules governing access of Russian nationals to Europe,” he said. “We are now stepping up our efforts towards a halt to all non-essential visas.

    “The strongest response Denmark can give is not to waver and to support Ukraine. And we fully intend to continue supporting Ukraine.”.

    According to Reuters, Rasmussen sent a message on Friday evening to senior European diplomats ‌proposing that the EU should halt tourist visas for Russian citizens and cease recognition of Russian non-biometric passports throughout the 29-nation Schengen free-travel zone.

    “We must take concrete actions that project European strength ‌and decisiveness,” the message stated. “There is clear momentum to act decisively now, and we should seize this moment to replace our current patchwork ​of national measures with a truly unified EU-wide approach.”.

    The note also urged each EU member state to offer Russians more limited visas that do not allow travel to other countries in the Schengen zone, and to set tougher entry restrictions for serving and former Russian soldiers.

    Police ⁠thwarted the alleged ⁠plot when ​they arrested three men with links to the Danish criminal underworld shortly before Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Viktorovich Vasiliev, was due to perform at a ⁠concert on 25 September, which was then cancelled, officials noted. Vasiliev holds US and Ukrainian nationality.

    Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, the head of Denmark’s national security and intelligence service, stated: “It is our clear assessment that the assassination attempt was planned by the Russian ⁠intelligence services.”.

    According to prosecutors, the suspects were driving towards the concert venue north of Copenhagen with two loaded pistols and two knives when police arrested them at about 9.55pm, five minutes before the concert was due ‌to begin. A fourth suspect was arrested later that evening, police mentioned.

    One of the suspects had bought a ticket to the concert, according ​to the charges.

    Recent findings suggest that the suspects are charged under Section 108 of Denmark’s criminal code, which covers assisting a foreign intelligence service, as well as attempted murder. They denied wrongdoing in court, the broadcaster DR reported.

    Kieffer-Kristensen said: “A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, ⁠and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and ​risk-taking Russia.

    “We believe ​that the case is key ​for understanding the threat that Denmark faces from Russia.”.

    Industry observers note that the European Commission president, Ursula ​von der Leyen, stated the EU ​stood in full solidarity with Denmark and with all member states targeted ​by Russian hybrid ‌attacks. She said the ​bloc would soon ​propose a “new European security strategy” to reinforce preparedness and deterrence.

    The Russian embassy ⁠in Copenhagen noted that Denmark’s accusations were not backed with ​proof.

    #82112. Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3697 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US.
    • In a recent development, the rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US.
    • While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn’t allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn’t been able to obtain an exemption.

    In a recent development, the rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.

    While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

    According to recent reports, TP-Link’s struggle is not much of a surprise, given its history as a Chinese company and the Trump administration’s focus on reducing reliance on Chinese and other foreign technology. While TP-Link faces political challenges related to the Trump administration’s push for on-shoring, its problems go deeper: It must convince the government its routers aren’t vulnerable to foreign hacking campaigns and that its routers are not Chinese-controlled technology, as suggested at a congressional committee hearing last year.

    It has been revealed that TP-Link was founded in 1996 in China but has since split into two companies, with one in the US. The US-based TP-Link established California as its global headquarters in October 2024, months after completing a “formal organizational separation” from the TP-Link entity in China.

    “TP-Link has split from and no longer has any affiliation with TP-LINK Technologies Co., Ltd., which serves the mainland Chinese market. Despite having similar names, these companies have entirely different ownership, management, and operations,” TP-Link says.

    TP-Link opened preorders for its first Wi-Fi 8 router, the Archer 8 Ultra, in September, though not in the US. It’s expected to ship this month and costs £899.99 in the UK, or about $1,178. Since it’s priced like a luxury device, its unavailability in the US won’t make a difference to most consumers. But it’s unknown how long it will take TP-Link to gain permission to sell Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, or whether it will receive permission at all.

    TP-Link has pledged to assemble all new routers in the US, but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task. The government reviews of router makers’ requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy. From the outside, it is unclear whether the Trump administration applies consistent security criteria to all companies or whether it grants waivers to favored companies without regard to the actual security of their products.

    Companies led by Trump allies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos fared well in the reviews. SpaceX’s Starlink division obtained a waiver for its routers, while Amazon received a waiver covering routers for its Leo satellite broadband service and the devices sold by its Eero subsidiary. There have been 26 waivers issued so far, covering products made by firms such as Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Calix, Nokia, Micro-Star International, Askey, Zyxel, Humax, and Vantiva.

    Some US lawmakers seem to think the FCC process covers too many products. House Commerce Committee Ranking Member Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-N.J.) and Chairman Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) proposed legislation in September that would limit the FCC’s authority to place entire categories of equipment on the list of banned products, as it did with routers.

    The Pallone/Guthrie bill would also require the FCC to report to Congress a week before adding any fresh technology or service to what’s known as the Covered List and require new additions to include only technologies or services produced or provided by an entity controlled by a foreign adversary. That means China, Russia, North Korea, or Iran.

    “The current process for identifying and barring malicious foreign technology has worked in many cases, but lacks the transparency, consistency, and clarity needed to meet our long-term national security needs as technology rapidly advances,” Pallone and Guthrie stated in a joint statement.

    It has been revealed that the Pentagon declined Ars’ request for comment on TP-Link’s request for an exemption. The FCC and Department of Homeland Security did not provide any comment.

    According to recent reports, the US ban on all foreign routers was part of a dramatic expansion of the Covered List, which is managed by the FCC in consultation with the Commerce Department and federal agencies with national security expertise. The Covered List was created by a 2020 law and received its first additions in March 2021. It applies to products that “pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”.

    Industry observers note that for the first few years of the Covered List’s existence, only specific companies were added. This included Chinese device-makers Huawei and ZTE, several video surveillance product makers, the Russian security tech giant Kaspersky Lab, and several Chinese telecom companies. Under the Trump administration, fresh additions to the list include entire product categories, regardless of whether a particular vendor has been identified as a risk. In addition to routers, the Covered List currently includes foreign drones, robotic devices, and power inverters.

    A former government official told Ars that the Covered List isn’t as useful as it should be.

    “The government needs to be able to quickly identify national security risks and, to the extent that they can, you’ve got to give the public and industry guidance on what to do in order to avoid that risk,” remarked Betsy McIntyre, a lawyer and consultant who previously worked for the FCC on telecom mergers and at the Department of Justice on national security reviews of foreign investment in telecom. “That’s why I have always loved the Covered List. It’s this great tool. It’s simple. It has so much potential to guide procurement decisions for small businesses, large businesses. It can even help when moms are going to Best Buy and figuring out what kinds of equipment they should be buying.”.

    McIntyre doesn’t like the approach of adding entire categories of products to the list, rather than specific products from individual companies.

    Industry observers note that “The ideal Covered List would be, as soon as there’s a problem, it would be updated,” she said. “They’d name a company, and then people know: ‘don’t buy this’ or ‘this kind of equipment poses a national security risk.’ It’s a little bit muddled now.”.

    Although the FCC maintains the Covered List, McIntyre said the FCC’s role was set up at the beginning to be “very ministerial.” The FCC would add companies or products to the list based on determinations by national security agencies, with the FCC having no discretion once it received a determination.

    In a recent development, mcIntyre noted that she was not privy to any of the discussions that led to the broad inclusion of routers this year. It’s not necessarily clear to the public why any particular item is added to the list or why any organization receives an exemption, because “the national security decision-making process can be a black box,” she stated.

    It has been revealed that TP-Link routers formed the bulk of a botnet controlled by Chinese threat actors, Microsoft mentioned in 2024. But TP-Link is far from the only router maker whose products have vulnerabilities. Routers made by US companies Cisco and Netgear were part of a botnet of devices hijacked by Chinese state-sponsored attackers in 2023, the Justice Department said after taking action to remove the malware.

    Recent findings suggest that security expert Bruce Schneier remarked there’s no reason to think TP-Link routers are less secure than those of its competitors. “They’re all awful. They’re all equally awful,” he told Ars.

    Computers and smartphones generally have strong security because companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft “have massive security teams designing these things to be good in the first place and writing patches when flaws are found,” Schneier mentioned.

    According to recent reports, with routers, webcams, smart refrigerators, wireless drones, and Internet of Things devices in general, “there’s no one on staff to deal with a security vulnerability… These are just less secure devices because the economics of them doesn’t reward security. The way you patch a lot of your home routers is you throw it away and buy a new one. That’s the patch mechanism.”.

    When asked about TP-Link facing more scrutiny because of its history as a Chinese company, Schneier said that router makers are “all Chinese companies… I don’t care what [name] you stick on the box. They’re all made in China.”.

    TP-Link is pledging to assemble routers in the US, though it would still use parts from overseas. Schneier said that “these are distinctions that don’t matter that much.”.

    TP-Link says the devices it sells in the US are made in Vietnam. But an April 2025 Bloomberg article remarked, “TP-Link confirmed that, aside from components bought in Vietnam that account for 0.5 percent of the total value of inputs to the plant there, all other components are imported from China.”.

    TP-Link declined an interview request from Ars this month. “Aside from what’s already out there, the manufacturer doesn’t have any new updates to share right now,” a TP-Link spokesperson told us.

    TP-Link could sue the government, but litigation can drag out for years. Drone makers have been subject to the same kind of FCC import ban since December 2025, and Chinese drone maker DJI sued the FCC in February. FCC and Justice Department lawyers urged the court to dismiss the lawsuit as “premature,” because the FCC hasn’t made a final decision on a petition that DJI filed with the FCC. The US government’s latest motion to dismiss the lawsuit is still pending with the Ninth Circuit appeals court, and the FCC hasn’t ruled on the petition for reconsideration that DJI filed in January.

    Several developments over the past two years make it unsurprising that TP-Link hasn’t obtained a waiver. US officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban due to national security risks during the final months of the Biden administration. The government separately probed TP-Link last year in an antitrust investigation reportedly focused on whether it sold goods below cost to gain a dominant share of the US router market.

    The House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party held a March 2025 hearing on deterring China’s hacking attacks and improving what the committee called “America’s lackluster cyber defenses.” Rob Joyce, former director of cybersecurity for the National Security Agency, said in testimony that China is “undercutting our market to deliver Chinese-controlled technologies into our homes” and named TP-Link as the prime example.

    “TP-Link, the world’s largest manufacturer of commercial Wi-Fi and home routers, has grown to at least 60 percent of the US retail market for Wi-Fi systems and SoHo [Small Office and Home Office] routers compared with about 10 percent of the market at the start of 2019,” he noted. “How have they achieved this miraculous growth? They appear to be selling at price points below profitability to drive out the western competition… TP-Link routers were among the various brands exploited by Chinese state-sponsored hackers in the massive Volt, Flax, and Salt Typhoon attacks… We cannot have the software for these prolific devices be written, updated, and controlled by a Chinese tech giant. By law, such a company is subject to the direction of the PRC [People’s Republic of China] Intelligence apparatus. This is a threat we cannot ignore.”.

    TP-Link noted in a March 2025 response to Joyce’s comments that its “products are not ‘Chinese-controlled technology,’” that “all of TP-Link’s R&D operations globally are owned and controlled by TP-Link’s US headquarters,” and that “no government—including the PRC—has access to and control over the design and production of TP-Link routers.”.

    In 2023, the year before Biden administration officials reportedly considered a TP-Link ban, TP-Link boasted of being “the world’s No. 1 Wi-Fi product provider for 12 years running” based on analyst firm IDC’s tracking of worldwide shipments. More recently, TP-Link has argued that estimates of its dominance are wildly inflated, at least in the US.

    TP-Link’s response to Joyce said it held “a 36.6 percent unit share and a 31 percent dollar share of the US consumer router market during 2024.” The company says in a fact sheet that when routers provided to owners by Internet service providers are taken into account, “TP-Link’s market share of residential Wi-Fi router sales in North America in 2024 was under 10 percent.”.

    Florida and three other states with Republican attorneys general sued TP-Link last month, alleging that it lied to consumers about connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers. A group of 21 Republican state AGs also sent a letter to the FCC, urging it to address alleged violations of state laws in its review of TP-Link’s waiver request. TP-Link told the FCC that the “heightened standard” demanded by state attorneys general “would be unattainable to TP-Link or any other router manufacturer in the world.”.

    It has been revealed that last month, the FCC warned TP-Link that several of its existing routers exceeded power limits. These include devices already being used by US consumers, such as the Archer BE670 tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router.

    “Based on our evaluation of the purchased samples, we have tentatively determined that TP-Link included false or incorrect information in its applications for these equipment authorizations; and these devices do not operate consistently with the parameters power levels [sic] submitted in the certification applications,” the FCC told TP-Link.

    In a recent development, TP-Link told Bloomberg that any routers exceeding power limits are an aberration and that the four products identified by the FCC account for less than one-third of 1 percent of the company’s total US unit sales this year. Nonetheless, the power-limit investigation related to TP-Link’s existing routers may be a bad sign for its chances of getting a waiver to import and sell Wi-Fi 8 routers.

    TP-Link told reporter Dong Ngo that the FCC tests were “routine spot checks.” But FCC officials may have examined existing TP-Link devices because of the pending request for a waiver from the Covered List.

    “Any time a company has significant requests before the agency, it’s not unusual if the agency is making sure that the company is behaving in a manner the way they expect it to, complying with the rules,” noted Jeremy Marcus, a lawyer who spent over 20 years in government in multiple roles, including deputy chief of the FCC Enforcement Bureau.

    Sources indicate that marcus declined to discuss TP-Link specifically. He noted that the FCC Office of Engineering and Technology has ongoing market surveillance programs. But when a company has larger problems pending at the FCC, the Office of Engineering and Technology may “do their own due diligence to make sure that existing equipment is performing the way it’s authorized to,” he noted.

    Although TP-Link has since gone a bit quiet and declined an interview request from Ars, a tech giant official previously spoke to other publications about the FCC waiver process. TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky told PCMag last month that “there isn’t a lot of clarity” in the government’s demands for US-built technology. Many components used in routers are only available from foreign countries, he mentioned.

    According to recent reports, “There are no published guidelines that say, ‘Well, it could be 25 percent US, or it could be 15 percent US,'” he stated. “Or what about, we buy our chipsets for these products from Qualcomm and Broadcom. Is that a US product?”.

    Kovsky’s background is in corporate marketing and communications, and he started at TP-Link a year ago in a contracting role as a senior communications strategist and consultant. He was hired as the corporate affairs officer in June and has been the main public speaker on the manufacturer’s attempts to get a Covered List waiver.

    According to recent reports, kovsky expressed some optimism last month. “We have no problem with the FCC, and are really looking forward to pursuing this, and really setting the standard for transparency, and showing that we have the ability to perform and meet all of these criteria with flying colors,” Kovsky told PCMag. “I don’t know if every manufacturer could say the same thing.”.

    Kovsky spoke to The Verge around the same time, defending the company’s security. “We do not sell customer data or share it with any government ever,” he stated. “We never will. We do not allow backdoors in our products. We are not susceptible to malware or vulnerabilities to an extent that’s greater than any other manufacturer in this category, to my knowledge.”.

    According to recent reports, kovsky also downplayed TP-Link’s router market share in the US. “It’s about 9 to 10 percent, which is like top three,” he said. “It’s a good number, but we do not have an overwhelming share of the US market.”.

    Sources indicate that kovsky pleaded with government officials for a quick approval in a letter to the FCC last month. TP-Link is ready to make “a nearly $1 billion investment in America that would result in equipping existing US factories, and ultimately building new, highly automated manufacturing facilities, to start assembling next-generation Wi-Fi 8 routers in the United States as soon as next year, creating hundreds of new jobs,” he wrote. “TP-Link is proud of this proposal and is poised to unleash this investment upon a grant of its Conditional Approval application.”.

    Because the Trump administration added virtually all routers to the Covered List, each router maker must obtain a determination from the Department of Defense or Department of Homeland Security that its routers do not pose unacceptable national security risks and present a blueprint to establish or expand manufacturing in the US.

    Router makers seeking conditional approvals must submit, among other things, details about which countries all of the components and software in its routers come from; details about parts that have only a single source and contingency plans if those suppliers become unavailable; locations of manufacturing and assembly; and a “quantitative assessment of supply chain concentration by country, expressed as both a percentage of total value and production volume.”.

    Router makers must also provide a “justification on why any foreign manufactured router is not currently manufactured in the United States, including why these foreign sources were selected and whether alternatives exist,” and a “detailed, time-bound strategy to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States.”.

    Although McIntyre would prefer that the list be focused on individual companies instead of entire product categories, she said others argue that the process benefits the US because it forces companies to think harder about where they obtain components from and to provide the government with on-shoring plans.

    “I have talked to people who say, ‘Listen, you do these entire class bans, and it’s really forcing companies to really think about their supply chain… You want to have as many of these routers made in the United States as possible, just because you have a little bit more control over what’s going into the router,’” she stated.

    The FCC mentioned the addition of routers was based on a determination by a White House-convened group of Executive Branch agencies with national security expertise, which said that “malicious state and non-state sponsored cyber attackers have increasingly leveraged the vulnerabilities in small and home office routers produced abroad to carry out direct attacks.” The agencies said that “routers in the United States must have trusted supply chains so we are not providing foreign actors with potential built-in backdoors to American homes, businesses, critical infrastructure, and emergency services.”.

    In a recent development, although the FCC has generally based Covered List inclusions on determinations by other agencies, McIntyre pointed out an exception. In January 2025, the Commerce Department issued a determination about the risk of connected car hardware and software being controlled by Chinese- or Russian-controlled entities and used its own authority to prohibit transactions involving Chinese or Russian vehicle-connectivity systems.

    After the Commerce determination, the FCC sought comment from the public on whether to add the vehicles to the Covered List. “That is the only example I have found of the FCC doing anything other than just taking what they were given and putting it on the Covered List,” McIntyre mentioned.

    Sources indicate that under the law, the FCC is required to base Covered List decisions on determinations by federal agencies with national security expertise, or the Department of Commerce. With connected cars, the FCC took public comment and has not added the vehicles to the list.

    “We are not required to provide the opportunity for public input on updates to the Covered List under the Commission’s rules, and we have not done so in the past,” the FCC mentioned in May 2025. “However, because this would be the first addition that does not include the names of specific entities, we believe that offering an opportunity for public input will help promote transparency and good governance.”.

    The FCC made its first Covered List addition that does not include names of specific entities seven months later, but for drones, not connected cars. The Pallone/Guthrie bill mentioned earlier in this article would limit or prevent future additions that don’t name specific entities.

    “The placement on or removal from the list… of a class or category of information and communications technology or service without reference to an entity that produced or provided that technology shall be deemed a major rule” as defined in the Congressional Review Act (CRA), the bill notes.

    It has been revealed that the CRA lets Congress overturn certain federal actions, including major rules. Pallone and Guthrie’s bill announcement said the Covered List process needs Congressional oversight and that their proposed “changes improve consistency and transparency around the FCC Covered List, ensuring that it targets foreign adversaries and is used as Congress intended to safeguard our national security.”.

    Tech Report: Tesla's assisted driving system gets the green light for rollout in Italy

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (206 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tesla’s self-driving tech is awaiting another major vote from the European Union before the end of the year.
    • In a recent development, italy's Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport has granted provisional approval for Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised), which has been rebranded to Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe.
    • Italy's approval notches another regulatory milestone for Tesla since the country decided to preempt the European Union's expected vote on its driver assistance system slated for later this year.

    Tesla’s self-driving tech is awaiting another major vote from the European Union before the end of the year.

    In a recent development, italy's Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport has granted provisional approval for Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised), which has been rebranded to Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe. The Tesla Europe account on X confirmed in a post that it's been approved in Italy, with the rollout beginning soon. It also highlighted off footage of Tesla Assisted Driving operating near The Coliseum and on Italian roads. Italy's minister of infrastucture and transport, Matteo Salvini, also posted on X that Tesla's driver assistance system has been given the green light after a "timely technical feasibility review.".

    Italy's approval notches another regulatory milestone for Tesla since the country decided to preempt the European Union's expected vote on its driver assistance system slated for later this year. Tesla is still awaiting decisions from other major European Union countries, including Germany and France, which is currently in the process of testing Tesla Assisted Driving.

    Tesla's self-driving tech first made its debut in Europe, thanks to the Dutch regulatory authority's provisional approval in April. Since then, several smaller European countries have followed suit, including Denmark, Belgium and Czechia.

    #82110. ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1146 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

    ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1146 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The ANC got the most votes overall but lost control in more than half of the councils it won in 2021.
    • The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.
    • The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worstâ¯result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The ANC got the most votes overall but lost control in more than half of the councils it won in 2021.

    The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.

    The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worstâ¯result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.

    Recent findings suggest that it won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.

    At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.

    Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.

    While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.

    But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.

    Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.

    It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.

    Recent findings suggest that the left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.

    In a recent development, it emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.

    The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.

    The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.

    Recent findings suggest that the two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).

    Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.

    Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.

    ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba (left) and ANC chairperson Gwede Mantashe (right) look set to reach on agreement on co-governing some of South Africa's biggest cities.

    The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.

    Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.

    In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.

    The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.

    ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.

    It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.

    While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.

    A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.

    While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.

    Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, mentioned that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".

    The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.

    While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.

    But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.

    Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.

    As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.

    This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.

    Experts agree that even after upcoming arrangements take effect, it will take longer than a five-year term to resolve the complications facing many municipalities, particularly South Africa's biggest city Johannesburg.

    "I think if we are really turning the ship around, we are talking about a 10-year period," Duvenhage remarked.

    Swana echoed this, saying it would take a decade to "cleanse and purify" local councils and "reinstate them as "proper municipalities".

    GTA 6 on Xbox Series S: How well it actually runs

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Reading through Reddit, there is no shortage of concerns about how well Xbox Series S will or won’t run the game.
    • In a recent development, how much time did I spend sweating the idea of crowd density?
    • And yet, while it filled me with regret for not buying a PS5 last Black Friday before the price hikes arrived, it did not stop me from buying GTA 6 on Xbox Series S, debating whether or not to resist the pull off the Latest Zealand timezone trick to play it early, and preparing to explore Leonida.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here.

    Reading through Reddit, there is no shortage of concerns about how well Xbox Series S will or won’t run the game. As the release neared, fans seemed confident that Rockstar Games would ensure the game was playable, but opinions varied widely on what graphical sacrifices would be required for it to run, including reduced crowd density and scaled-back visuals.

    In a recent development, how much time did I spend sweating the idea of crowd density? Too much. Did I ever think about it or care about it until Redditors noted it’ll likely be less on the Series S? Not at all.

    And yet, while it filled me with regret for not buying a PS5 last Black Friday before the price hikes arrived, it did not stop me from buying GTA 6 on Xbox Series S, debating whether or not to resist the pull off the Latest Zealand timezone trick to play it early, and preparing to explore Leonida.

    And now, having played GTA 6 for a few hours, I can tell you everything you need to know about how it runs and how it feels.

    According to recent reports, I won’t keep you waiting: GTA 6 runs smooth as butter on Xbox Series S. There were no stutters, no lag or other slowdowns that pulled me out of the gameplay.

    During a prologue that introduced me to protagonists Jason and Lucia, I swiftly experienced a variety of locations in daytime and nighttime, as well as rainy weather. After that, I was able to play around Leonida and check out all the basic things that might catch your attention as you play: how the weather looks, flying down the road in a car through busy streets, random tasks around Jason's home.

    In addition to moving quickly through various areas, I also took a moment to slow down. I watched a sunset by the water, went for a swim surrounded by fish, and observed how the environment affected Jason. Nothing slowed down, glitched out, or made me think anything other than I was playing a AAA game.

    What I can’t tell you right now is how much better GTA 6 is or isn’t on PS5 or any of the higher-end consoles. We’re in the process of comparing the Xbox Series S version to the PS5 Pro version as we speak.

    Sources indicate that rockstar has explicitly noted the game will run best on PS5 consoles, with faster load times and technology that may improve resolution. The PS5 Pro version will also include ray tracing, making the lighting even more eye-catching. But both games will still be locked at 30 frames per second, according to Rockstar. The game developer did not say if any other sacrifices had to be made to get it to run on the Xbox Series S.

    Recent findings suggest that regardless, what I can tell you is there is a good game waiting for you to play on Xbox Series S. If you don’t have the funds to upgrade your console, do not let comparison be the thief of joy.

    GTA 6 is a generational moment in gaming and a cultural moment much larger than any game launch I’ve ever seen. The game is fun, the music is a vibe, and the world is immersive without feeling like a chore. I can't imagine waiting to play this if they have the means to do so right now.

    Man convicted of arson over deadly 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A US-French man has been convicted on federal arson charges connected with the 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles, California, which killed 12 people and devastated the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades.
    • The weeks-long blaze destroyed some 6,800 homes and other structures, causing estimated property losses of $150 billion (€136.7 billion).
    • A US District Court jury in Los Angeles found the man guilty of starting a hilltop brush fire on January 1, 2025.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A US-French man has been convicted on federal arson charges connected with the 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles, California, which killed 12 people and devastated the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades.

    The weeks-long blaze destroyed some 6,800 homes and other structures, causing estimated property losses of $150 billion (€136.7 billion).

    A US District Court jury in Los Angeles found the man guilty of starting a hilltop brush fire on January 1, 2025.

    While the fire was initially suppressed, it continued smoldering underground and reignited days later amid fierce winds to become the highly destructive Palisades Fire.

    According to recent reports, the man is set to be sentenced on March 17. First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli told reporters that he could face up to 40 years in prison.

    The man was arrested in October 2025, and already faced one trial five months ago that ended with a hung jury. The judge declared a mistrial in June, prompting federal prosecutors to retry the case under modified charges.

    Prosecutors stated security camera footage and location data from the defendant's cellphone showed he was the only person nearby when ​the January 1 blaze began in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.

    At both trials, they characterized the man, a former Uber driver, as a loner who held a deep resentment against society, and particularly the wealthy.

    The defense argued that the initial blaze could have been caused by fireworks, while prosecutors said there was no evidence that any had been set off in the area.

    In March, the man denied in a court declaration that he had willfully started any fire, though he declined to testify in ⁠his own defense at either trial.

    The Palisades blaze erupted almost at the same time as another wildfire that broke out in Eaton Canyon, some 30 miles (48 km) to the east.

    That fire, believed to have been ignited by sparks from an electrical transmission tower, killed 19 people and devastated the Los Angeles suburb of Altadena.

    Together, the two blazes rank as the deadliest wildfire disaster ever seen in Los Angeles County.

    #82105. How to use a solar panel to charge your phone

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (592 w)

    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    How to use a solar panel to charge your phone

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Panel-only chargers, built-in batteries and portable power stations all work differently, so here's how to find the right fit.
    • It has been revealed that when you're out hiking, far away from an electrical outlet or stuck in a power outage, having a backup power bank for your phone and other devices makes sense.
    • According to recent reports, while there's a whole range of solar-powered chargers on the market, you can find smaller, lighter ones that can recharge devices like phones and laptops.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Panel-only chargers, built-in batteries and portable power stations all work differently, so here's how to find the right fit.

    It has been revealed that when you're out hiking, far away from an electrical outlet or stuck in a power outage, having a backup power bank for your phone and other devices makes sense. But a power bank will eventually run out, possibly leaving you with a phone battery in the red. If you're looking to prevent the inevitable panic that comes with a dead phone, a solar panel charger might be an option for you.

    According to recent reports, while there's a whole range of solar-powered chargers on the market, you can find smaller, lighter ones that can recharge devices like phones and laptops. They might be a good fit, particularly if you're on the move. You'll have a few decisions to make about the type of charger that works best for you, as well as the features you'll want, like charging ports and safety protections. Whether you're heading out on a camping trip or just looking to bypass the electrical grid, here's what you need to know about charging your phone with a portable solar charger.

    There are several types of solar-powered charging devices to pick from, and the one you get will largely depend on what you're going to use it for. A panel-only charger lets you plug a device like a phone directly into it. The panels convert sunlight into power, but there's no other way to store that power once it's been captured. A panel-only charger might be better suited for shorter-term use, particularly if it's sunny out.

    Industry observers note that other chargers come with built-in batteries, so you can store energy and use it later, creating an extra layer of convenience. If you're camping for a few days, for example, this duo of panels and battery could make it easier to stay charged and give you more control of when you do the charging.

    Finally, you can spring for a portable power station. While different models will have different features and capacities, a power station will generally let you charge several devices at the same time. It will also have battery storage. It may not be as easy to tote around as the others, but there are some compact units on the market weighing as little as 4 pounds.

    When you're deciding on a portable solar charger, there are a few considerations you want to make. For one, there's wattage. A model that's smaller and lighter-weight might be able to produce 15-50 watts. This range should work fine for charging smaller devices like your phone. It's notable to remember that the wattage will be impacted by variables like cloud cover or how the device is angled toward the sun, so you might not always get the wattage listed on the packaging. These factors will change charging time too.

    In a recent development, in addition, consider the number of ports that come with a portable solar charger. Some solar panel chargers will let you plug your phone directly into them with a USB-C port. Also think about how you'll be using it. A bigger, bulkier solar charging device might be harder to lug around if you're camping or hiking. Some chargers fold, making them easier to carry, or have stands that will help you better position the panels toward the sun. Others can clip to a backpack. Finally, be mindful of safety features like water and weather resistance, overcharge protection and temperature control.

    • Joshua Foster tells of moment he ‘lost control’ of two-year-old when he fell from fourth storey of hotel.
    • A British father who was fined by the courts after his two-year-old son fell from a fourth-floor window during a family holiday in Cyprus has recalled his “despair” when the boy slipped from his grasp.
    • Sources indicate that joshua Foster was handed a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty after he pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Joshua Foster tells of moment he ‘lost control’ of two-year-old when he fell from fourth storey of hotel.

    A British father who was fined by the courts after his two-year-old son fell from a fourth-floor window during a family holiday in Cyprus has recalled his “despair” when the boy slipped from his grasp.

    Sources indicate that joshua Foster was handed a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty after he pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. Prosecutors in Cyprus had refused to drop the case against him.

    During recent court proceedings, it was heard that Foster thought the window at the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas was closed when he approached it with his son, Jaxon, to show him the view of a waterpark.

    Sources indicate that the 37-year-old “lost control” of him, the Paphos district court was told, before the boy plunged 10 metres (33ft). The fall happened on 12 July, the first day of the Fosters’ family holiday.

    It has been revealed that in an interview with the Daily Mail, Foster stated: “I have a burden. I’ll have that my whole life. It’s very traumatic. My mind doesn’t want to go there. I just remember the despair of him falling, and watching him fall.

    “It was just such a shock … I put him up thinking he was going against a glass pane … and then he wasn’t there.”.

    The toddler was pronounced dead at Paphos general hospital shortly after he suffered severe cranial injuries when he hit a veranda below.

    It has been revealed that foster recalled his outpouring of emotion when he located his son after the fall. “I picked him up. I held him and screamed,” he said. The Essex-born auditor said he and his wife had an hour with their son’s body after he was pronounced dead.

    The decision to charge Foster, reported to be a senior accountant at KPMG, was criticised by his legal representatives, as well as human rights defenders, media pundits and diplomats, arguing that it lacked compassion.

    The charge Foster accepted is usually levelled in cases involving fatal traffic accidents. It carries a maximum penalty of four years in prison, but the fine he was handed was the lightest sentence possible for the offence.

    At his sentencing in October, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, before describing the incident as a “tragic event”.

    The court had heard that, while the presence of alcohol had been detected in Foster’s blood, it was not enough to suggest he was impaired to the point where he had “acted recklessly”.

    According to recent reports, foster was detained after the fall. He reportedly had to tell his eldest child, a daughter, about her brother’s death via a video call while he was being held.

    He posted €30,000 (£26,000) in bail to return to the UK to attend the funeral of his son in August, but was forced, under threat of extradition, to return to Cyprus and surrender his passport by 14 September.

    In a push for clemency, Foster’s legal team had appealed in September to the island’s attorney general, Cyprus’s top legal official, to discontinue the criminal procedure on humanitarian grounds. The request was denied.

    Since returning home, Foster mentioned the focus of his grieving family had turned to their daughter.

    “It’s very difficult,” he mentioned. “She waves at the sky and states: ‘I love you’ to him and blows a kiss. She’s lost her best friend. She’s gone from having a sibling to being an only child.”.
