    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mildred Juarez was stuck in detention for a month after her friends sent her bail money to Libre Immigration Services.

    Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.

    But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.

    Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (Â£1,970) to a bond tech giant, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS stated it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.

    In a recent development, what she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.

    Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail organization in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.

    But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.

    Industry observers note that since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.

    Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.

    "He did everything right" - The impact of Trump's immigration crackdown in Ohio.

    Industry observers note that in the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.

    The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

    For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.

    According to recent reports, in an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.

    An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the organization had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.

    But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another firm.

    "I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.

    In a recent development, "I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside.".

    Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund. A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.

    It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.

    Industry observers note that once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.

    It has been revealed that bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.

    Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.

    Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.

    Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

    Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.

    Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.

    A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.

    Rosa Murillo says she was ashamed to wear the ankle bracelet that Nexus required.

    Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private tech giant's requirement.

    Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.

    Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.

    But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.

    A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.

    When Mark Supetran worked for Libre by Nexus, he indicates he would tell people about how they had to wear an ankle bracelet.

    But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the firm for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.

    Sources indicate that supetran stated he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation.

    According to recent reports, "Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government.".

    Sources indicate that not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed.

    In a recent development, "But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'".

    Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could problem no refund.

    The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent firm.

    The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.

    The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the company liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.

    In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the manufacturer from collecting on past debts.

    Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.

    As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.

    Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.

    Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.

    The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.

    Smith called the new business Libre Immigration Services.

    This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.

    According to recent reports, judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.

    According to recent reports, A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She said after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.

    Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.

    A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the manufacturer was never in possession of the client lists.

    A screenshot of Libre Immigration Service's website.

    Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.

    Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".

    That wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles remarked, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.

    When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she remarked.

    Eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.

    She said the tech giant finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.

    An LIS spokesperson mentioned that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss".

    "The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review.".

    They also said the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.

    Recent findings suggest that but the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention. "I'm like 'This ain't right.'".

    #82100. Six simple Raspberry Pi projects for beginners

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1156 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Six simple Raspberry Pi projects for beginners

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Stop leaving your Pi builds unfinished with these fun and useful ideas.
    • Raspberry Pi projects are infamous for fizzling out before completion.
    • Industry observers note that even Raspberry Pis haven't been spared from RAMageddon.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stop leaving your Pi builds unfinished with these fun and useful ideas.

    Raspberry Pi projects are infamous for fizzling out before completion. Sure, the truly dedicated will finish things like custom voice assistants, irrigation systems or creepy animatronics. However, many Pi projects end up requiring more patience than beginners are willing to invest. Here are a few ideas that should be easy enough to prevent your purchase from collecting dust.

    Industry observers note that even Raspberry Pis haven't been spared from RAMageddon. With AI data centers gobbling up the world's memory supply, we've seen several Pi price increases since late 2025. The 16GB Pi 5 now costs $385, over three times its original $120 MSRP. A Pi is no longer the impulse purchase it once was.

    Recent findings suggest that mini PCs also fell victim to the RAM crisis, but they're still worth considering for some projects. A fully loaded Pi can cost at least as much as a small Intel mini PC, which will be faster and better at running regular PC software.

    Sources indicate that but if you don't need a particularly powerful computer, budget Pi models can still be had for cheap. The 1GB Pi 5, for example, still costs just $45. It can handle several of the following projects without issue, while the still-affordable 2GB or 4GB models will work for the rest.

    In a recent development, instead of installing ad blockers for every device in your home (and resigning yourself to the fact that streaming boxes and smart TVs probably won't have one), you can roll your own network-wide ad blocker. Pi-hole blocks ads and trackers for every device on the network. It's no surprise that it's one of the most popular entry points into Raspberry Pi wizardry: It's relatively straightforward for a beginner and it does something almost everyone can get behind.

    The software is free and open source, and it relies on third-party lists of known trackers and ad servers to function. The simplest setup is to plug a Pi directly into your router using an Ethernet cable. Of course, it will work elsewhere as long as it's on the same network as your router and configured properly. It just needs a fixed IP address and some tweaking to make sure your router hands out Pi-hole as your network's DNS server.

    In a recent development, A Pi can serve as the brains of an old-school gaming machine. You can flash software like Recalbox, Batocera or RetroPie to a microSD card and enjoy a menu of classic console and arcade emulators. You don't need much RAM for older platforms like NES or Sega Genesis, but you'll want 4GB or more (and a Pi 5) if you want the option of playing some GameCube and Wii titles.

    In addition to the Pi and microSD, you'll need a game controller, power supply and video cable (usually micro HDMI to HDMI). Remember that the software doesn't come with games, so you'll need to provide your own ROMs (and be OK with whatever legal gray areas may be involved). Although this setup is a bit more complicated than Pi-hole, the old-school, interactive reward at the end should provide enough incentive to stick with it.

    Recent findings suggest that if you want to take things a step further, you could even tackle a retro gaming handheld project. But unless you're truly hardcore about this, that's veering closer to "too complex to finish" territory, especially with pre-made ones being relatively affordable.

    Industry observers note that although it won't help with streaming services, this setup can make it easy to enjoy the movies, shows and music you already own. Software like LibreELEC can boot your Pi into Kodi, a TV-friendly UI for your digital media library. Kodi can host music, movies, shows, photos, live TV and even some games, and it has a library of customizable skins.

    Sources indicate that you'll need to set it up to access the files on a hard drive or home server. After doing so, Kodi should fill in most of the artwork and episode info on its own, and there's a library of free community-built add-ons to peruse. You probably won't even need a separate remote to control your Kodi setup, as a feature called HDMI-CEC lets you navigate it with the one you already have for your TV.

    According to recent reports, you can recreate the functionality of Google's discontinued Chromecast Audio using a Pi. If you don't remember Chromecast Audio, it was a small dongle that plugged into the audio input of a stereo or powered speakers. It essentially turned any "dumb" speaker into a wireless one.

    Sources indicate that to set it up, plug your Pi into an old stereo or powered speaker, then install Raspotify for Spotify Connect (Premium required) or Shairport Sync for AirPlay. The Pi-infused speaker will then come up as an audio output option in Spotify's device list or your iPhone's AirPlay menu.

    This isn't to be confused with a regular Chromecast, which was designed for video streaming and discontinued in 2024, replaced with the Google TV Streamer. Miming a Chromecast is a more complicated project, since video platforms tend to strictly police copy protection. Besides, a cheap streaming stick will do a better job anyway.

    A Pi doesn't just help you play retro games; it can also serve as a client for some of the most power-hungry modern titles on the market. You can play your PC games from the couch with a Pi project that resembles the (also discontinued) Steam Link box. It's called Sunshine, and while it's no Steam Machine replacement, this local-streaming solution plays well with your existing PC library and costs significantly less than $1,000.

    You'll need to install Sunshine on your PC (free, and compatible with NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs) and its companion software Moonlight on the Pi. Then, pair them with a PIN and enjoy your PC gaming library on the TV. However, it's worth noting that you'll want to put both the PC and Pi on wired connections if you can. Although this setup works over Wi-Fi, Ethernet is the more reliable option for local streaming.

    Recent findings suggest that your child's first computer probably doesn't need to be tricked out with a GeForce RTX 5090 — or anything even remotely close to that. A Raspberry Pi provides all the horsepower you need for an early learning experience.

    One dead-simple option is the Raspberry Pi 500, a Pi built into a keyboard. Plugging it into a monitor gives you a basic desktop with a web browser and coding tools. However, its RAMageddon-induced price of $180 makes it less attractive than it used to be.

    Just know that the Raspberry Pi 500 won't provide any parental controls out of the box. So, you'll want to spend some time on that before getting started, especially if your child will be using it unsupervised.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I’d like to stay here!
    • Recent findings suggest that but I’d rather make a case for why you’ll benefit from supporting Ars.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It’s now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica. It has been the only home I’ve known as a writer, and it has been essential to my development from scientist to blogger to journalist. It’s no exaggeration to say that Ars has helped make me who I am today.

    So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I’d like to stay here! Jobs that give you this sort of independence, that let you both edit and write, are very rare in journalism, and I’m unlikely to find another. Helping secure Ars’ future through your support will mean I don’t have to.

    Recent findings suggest that but I’d rather make a case for why you’ll benefit from supporting Ars. In fact, I’ll make three: the writing, the people, and the community.

    Sources indicate that since my start here, the central mission of Ars has been the same: cover the news in a way that helps our readers understand the facts and why they’re important. The landscape has shifted dramatically over that time—technology, science, and policy are very different from 21 years ago. But understanding those changes and why they happened matters. It matters for everything from what you should buy today to what the world you’re going to be living in 10 years from now will look like.

    Recent findings suggest that I’ve had the privilege of helping to decide how to translate that mission to science coverage. That decision took place against an important backdrop: While most people value things like evidence and research, they often struggle to recognize how those are used to build a body of reliable scientific information. That struggle kind of made the decision for me. Putting people in the know means helping them understand how science works as a process, and why that can produce information about the world we can trust.

    It has been revealed that focusing on that has made our science coverage different from most of what you can get elsewhere. We don’t just tell you what’s fresh in the world of science; we help you understand the history of the massive questions, the breakthroughs that allow us to address old problems in new ways, and the clever ideas people have for how to extract reliable information from a noisy and chaotic Universe. I’d like to think our readers get more out of that sort of writing, and it’s worth supporting.

    In a recent development, but I’d be giving you a very incomplete picture of things if I only talked about science. Everyone at Ars has had to think about what sort of stories and presentation fit best with our mission. While our writing is essential now, it’s the people behind it that will ensure that it remains vital no matter what other changes come our way in the coming decades. And I can say with more than a little confidence that Ars is full of people you can trust to keep it that way.

    One reason you can trust that is that the people at Ars now are, in many cases, the same ones who were here when you first started reading the site. We have remarkably low turnover, especially at the higher levels in our organization. There are two reasons for that: Ars is incredibly well-managed, and the people here believe in our mission.

    The former is vital because it should assure you that the money we get from your subscription won’t be wasted on some ill-advised pivot to video, or whatever the next craze is. The latter matters because it’s the people here who make Ars what it is. I work with some of the most thoughtful people I have ever encountered, and they all care deeply about making our work informative and compelling. I have also been lucky enough to work with a large group of freelancers over the years, and I have nothing but good things to say about them. We work hard to make sure that, even when the name on the byline is unfamiliar to you, you can be confident that you’re getting the same quality of reporting.

    It has been revealed that all of them—the full-time staff and the freelancers—are smart, great writers and know their areas of expertise better than most people in this business. Like I’m sure you do, I learn a lot from what they write (unlike you, I also get the bonus of learning from them in our Slack channels).

    It has been revealed that but it’s not just my fellow writers whom I’ve learned from. We’ve got one of the smartest communities on the Internet, with experts from pretty much every area we cover regularly contributing to the comments. In the discussions attached to my articles, I have regularly seen them fill in details I didn’t have space to mention, clarify things in response to other readers’ questions, and talk about related topics that didn’t really fit into the article. I’ve learned a lot from this, and I’m confident the rest of the readers have, too.

    Industry observers note that it’s strange to say the opposite of one of the central dogmas of the Internet: Read the comments. But it’s something I’ve told our freelance writers pretty regularly.

    We’ve kept things that way even as most other sites’ comments turned toxic and were shut off. That’s taken both an editorial commitment and lots of staff time spent moderating and engaging in community management. Those don’t come for free, so your subscriptions will help support that, too.

    In a recent development, I hope you’ll consider signing up if you’re able. Beyond the financials, I know we all appreciate it as a sign we’re on the right track.

    Industry News: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’.
    • Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
    • Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’.

    Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.

    Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.

    The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.

    Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.

    It has been revealed that some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.

    The US remarked the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.

    South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a latest law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.

    The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any newly introduced laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.

    Recent findings suggest that the Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”.

    Diplomats inside the negotiations mentioned Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.

    The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.

    Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.

    Critics remarked this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.

    One European diplomat mentioned: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”.

    A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, noted autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.

    A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.

    On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”.

    #82093. Which car has the largest infotainment touchscreen?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (586 w)

    EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Which car has the largest infotainment touchscreen?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The biggest infotainment screen on the market keeps drivers and passengers connected.
    • Sources indicate that car infotainment screens are huge right now — both literally and figuratively.
    • Industry observers note that while most infotainment screens are embedded in the dashboard, the biggest screens instead take over the whole thing, stretching nearly from one side to the other.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The biggest infotainment screen on the market keeps drivers and passengers connected.

    Sources indicate that car infotainment screens are huge right now — both literally and figuratively. New cars have overwhelmingly embraced Android Auto and Apple CarPlay-powered infotainment screens in place of physical buttons, using them to display everything from GPS navigation and music controls to backup camera feeds. As these screens' importance and functionality have grown, so have the screens themselves, with some reaching truly enormous proportions.

    Industry observers note that while most infotainment screens are embedded in the dashboard, the biggest screens instead take over the whole thing, stretching nearly from one side to the other. That's the case with the massive 56-inch screen of the Mercedes-Benz EQS 580 4MATIC, the biggest infotainment screen you can get in a car. Technically, it comprises three separate screens (one each in front of the driver's seat, center console and passenger seat), all of which sit under a single, dash-spanning glass panel.

    Recent findings suggest that dubbed the Hyperscreen by Mercedes, the panel packs a huge array of functions, putting standard controls like media volume alongside more specialized features. One of the touted benefits of its massive size is that the Hyperscreen can display every control a driver might need at once, meaning you won't have to scroll through menus to find one. The size lets the screen keep a map and media controls displayed at all times, but there's more to it than screen real estate: Mercedes-Benz also has what it calls a zero-layer interface, which changes the apps displayed at any given time based on factors like the time of day and which apps you use the most often.

    Recent findings suggest that the Hyperscreen's dashboard-spanning size also comes in handy by putting a screen right in front of the passenger seat. From there, the passenger can use the car's media features, including watching YouTube videos, without interfering with the driver's display. Passengers can also help navigate by looking up destinations and planning routes on their screen, then sending those to the main navigation display for the driver to follow.

    In a recent development, mercedes-Benz's OS offers seven configurable passenger-seat profiles, letting individual passengers set what appears on their screen by default. To reduce distracted driving, the passenger screen only works when someone is in the seat, and a built-in sensor dims or turns it off if it detects the driver looking at it.

    In a recent development, whether all that screen real estate really helps when driving is an open question, though. While the Hyperscreen's size offers some advantages, it can also be a huge distraction, even with the automaker's attempts to stop drivers from staring at the passenger screen. And despite Mercedes' claims that its zero-layer interface will keep drivers from navigating complicated menus, some reviewers have found that the all-capacitive controls can be a pain to use in real-world conditions. Given its dash-spanning size, drivers also have to contend with the steering wheel obscuring some of the screen, which isn't a problem for smaller, center-mounted displays.

    In a recent development, beyond those issues specific to the EQS 580, it also suffers from problems intrinsic to touchscreens, like their propensity for collecting fingerprints. Some drivers also find touchscreens harder to use than physical buttons, a problem that's multiplied with the EQS since the Hyperscreen replaces almost every physical control. There's plenty of impressive tech behind the Mercedes EQS 580, but bigger might not always be better for infotainment screens.

    #82091. Latest Update: The Outages Are Just Getting Started

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1269 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: The Outages Are Just Getting Started

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1269 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network.
    • Recent findings suggest that so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations.
    • Sources indicate that AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

    Recent findings suggest that so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

    Sources indicate that AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to promptly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

    Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed patch in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials stated this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

    External pressures and bugs in patches are not latest, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

    “Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” states Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”.

    IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.

    “AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar issues elsewhere,” notes Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”.

    Matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These newly introduced threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.

    In a recent development, still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000. To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.

    In the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the organization that had been discovered by researchers using AI.

    There are important nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik states. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”.

    Only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher, at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.

    Recent findings suggest that “What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” indicates Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”.

    Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.

    • Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some company data. The bank states “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters. The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.

    It has been revealed that • Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech tech giant was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “wrench attacks”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage.

    Industry observers note that • Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports, the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

    Sources indicate that spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

    Here is a roundup of the main headlines from India on Saturday, November 21 and Sunday, November 22:.

    We're logging off today, but we will be back tomorrow with the latest from across India.

    Workers of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC), the youth wing of the opposition Indian National Congress, protested at US tech giant Meta's offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram on Friday, demanding that the group's leaders' Instagram accounts be restored.

    In Hyderabad, protesters entered the building, smashed plants and clashed with police, according to footage the IYC released. Meta declined to comment.

    The IYC said Instagram withheld the accounts of its president and in-charge on November 19 "on BJP orders," referring to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, and restored both shortly after the protests.

    Manu Jain, who runs the group's social media, told Reuters thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted.

    BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari noted: "Congress is a party of goons! Goons of Indian Youth Congress are not only vandalized and destroyed Meta's office in Hyderabad, & also are flaunting it on social media!".

    Meanwhile, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav warned foreign companies against getting involved in Indian politics.

    Recent findings suggest that the Indian government claims it orders takedowns only for content that breaches local laws or threatens public safety or national security. In February, it cut the deadline for removing unlawful content from 36 hours to three.

    Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in the previous six months, saying most were cases where local law required it to restrict content proactively.

    Recent findings suggest that earlier this month, Brazil’s top electoral court fined Meta's Facebook $1.3 million for failing to comply with judicial orders during the country's presidential election runoff campaign. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's team accused the company of political bias.

    According to recent reports, india closed day three of the first Test against Latest Zealand on 486-4, a lead of 118 runs. KL Rahul made 136, Shubman Gill 98 and Rishabh Pant was unbeaten on 55 as every one of India's top five passed 50.

    Recent findings suggest that rahul reached his 13th Test hundred off 207 balls, batting for more than eight hours and sharing stands of 165 with Devdutt Padikkal (80) and 91 with Gill. It completed a set of Test centuries in every major Test-playing nation outside the subcontinent for the Indian wicketkeeper-batsman.

    "It feels really awesome, actually, to be able to achieve something like that," Rahul noted.

    Industry observers note that he survived an LBW appeal on 5 that was given not out and New Zealand chose not to review. "Those 15 seconds were probably the slowest 15 seconds of my life," he said of the review process.

    Gill and Pant added 100 in the final session before Gill was bowled by Jacob Duffy just before stumps. Duffy finished with 1-180 from 29 overs, the fourth most expensive figures in New Zealand's Test history, AFP said.

    The pitch, green on day one, flattened out. "We expected a lot of grass on the wicket, we expected a lot of movement and it has probably not panned out that way," Padikkal noted.

    Fresh Zealand were all out for 368 in their first innings.

    The two-match series ends next week in Christchurch.

    At least 14 people have died and more than 200 have been hospitalized after drinking suspected adulterated liquor in Manipur's Chandel district.

    At least 12 people remain in critical condition, local media reported.

    The victims drank the liquor in the Chakpikarong area, about 75 kilometers (47 miles) from the state capital city of Imphal, and deaths were reported between November 18 and 20.

    Industry observers note that chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh visited the hospitals where most patients were being treated on Friday. He ordered an inquiry and stated the culprits would be arrested soon.

    It has been revealed that police remarked the liquor came from Sugnu in neighboring Kakching district, with no known local brewing in Chandel. A case has been filed, and two people have been arrested.

    The local administration has advised residents not to drink liquor from questionable sources and asked anyone who consumed liquor from the same source to get a medical check-up, even without symptoms.

    A US federal judge sentenced an Indian national on Friday to 19 years and seven months in prison for plotting to hire a hitman to kill Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.

    Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

    "I'm sorry to Mr. Pannun," he mentioned in court. Judge Victor Marrero said he faces deportation to India after serving his sentence.

    Prosecutors say an Indian government employee recruited Gupta in 2023. The government employee remains overseas and is not in US custody.

    Gupta paid $15,000 (€13,670) to a person he believed was a hitman, who was actually an undercover US agent.

    Prosecutors also said Gupta had told that agent the day after Hardeep Singh Nijjar's June 2023 killing in Canada that Nijjar "was also the target," the Associated Press reported.

    His lawyer, Isabelle Kirshner, denied he had any role in the Nijjar killing.

    "There is no question he was not the brains behind this operation," she noted. Canada has separately alleged India arranged Nijjar's killing, and India dismissed that, with both countries expelling diplomats.

    Sources indicate that india denies any involvement in the Pannun plot. Fresh Delhi has designated Pannun a terrorist.

    Pannun, who leads the group Sikhs for Justice, called Gupta a foot soldier and said outside court: "I'm ready to face India's bullet if that is the price I have to pay.".

    #82087. How does iCloud Private Relay's security compare to VPN alternatives?

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    How does iCloud Private Relay's security compare to VPN alternatives?

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • iCloud Private Relay and VPNs protect your browsing in different ways.
    • It has been revealed that apple's Private Relay is one of the extras you get by subscribing to an iCloud+ blueprint, alongside extra storage and other features like Hide My Email.
    • Think of iCloud Private Relay as two separate layers that protect your web browsing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    iCloud Private Relay and VPNs protect your browsing in different ways.

    It has been revealed that apple's Private Relay is one of the extras you get by subscribing to an iCloud+ blueprint, alongside extra storage and other features like Hide My Email. At first glance, iCloud Private Relay looks like an Apple VPN, as it hides your IP address from the websites you visit to keep your browsing data private. But Private Relay doesn't offer the same level of protection as a VPN; it doesn't encrypt everything and, more importantly, only works in Safari.

    Think of iCloud Private Relay as two separate layers that protect your web browsing. Apple runs the first layer and sees your original IP address, but not the website you're visiting. A partner like Cloudflare or Akamai operates the second layer and connects you to the website without knowing where the request came from. Neither Apple nor the partner has the full picture of your browsing history, making it much harder for websites to track you across the web.

    Private Relay's major limitations are that it only works with Safari and app traffic sent over unencrypted HTTP. Everything else bypasses Private Relay, including browsing activity from other web browsers and apps. Private Relay isn't untraceable either, since websites get an IP address that corresponds to your general region, with no way to choose a different location to bypass geo-blocking. Using passkeys with Private Relay also exposes your real IP address, since the request is made outside the browser. Apple was investigating the concern as of August 2026, and it's something to keep in mind if you're especially privacy-conscious.

    iCloud Private Relay also isn't available worldwide and doesn't work in countries like China, Russia and Saudi Arabia. That makes it less than ideal if you initiative to protect your browsing history while traveling. Even if you can use Private Relay, you may still encounter some website compatibility problems with it enabled.

    It has been revealed that unlike Private Relay, a regular VPN encrypts everything leaving your device, regardless of the app or browser. You can also set it up on other devices, such as a Windows computer or an Android phone. Some VPNs can even be set up directly on your router, so that they protect your entire connection. They also let you switch IP addresses and change locations whenever you want to bypass geo-fenced content. It's usually the easiest way to access a streaming catalog from another country or download something that isn't available in your region.

    You will have to trust the VPN provider, though. All your traffic goes through that one tech giant, so choosing an unknown VPN service could make your data even more vulnerable. If you're looking for a good VPN to use on your iPhone, stick with well-known services like ProtonVPN or ExpressVPN, and avoid using free ones from unknown developers. Some malware apps have posed as free VPNs, while malicious developers can track and sell your browsing data to advertisers.

    You can also use both iCloud Private Relay and a VPN at the same time. Keep Private Relay turned on when browsing with Safari, then switch to a VPN when you use other apps, browse on public Wi-Fi or are in a country where Private Relay doesn't work.

    Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.
    • This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.
    • In the fresh lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate.

    This Florida case adds to an already complex subplot involving Indigenous tribes, some of which are challenging prediction markets, while others are trying to get in on the action themselves.

    In the fresh lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal” in Florida.

    The tribe argues that every such “wager that Defendants now accept through their illegal sportsbook siphons away revenue that funds both the Tribe’s and Florida’s public programs and government services.”.

    Neither DraftKings nor its attorneys immediately responded to Ars’ request for comment. However, in a court filing, DraftKings says that its products available to Floridians are merely “fantasy sports and the trading of [financial] derivatives” and not gambling.

    DraftKings notes that its “licensed sportsbook” operates in other states but “not in Florida.”.

    Multiple companies, including DraftKings, claim that their “swaps” (a type of financial derivative) are, in fact, properly governed by a federal agency, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. Therefore, DraftKings argues, states cannot regulate this activity as gambling.

    It has been revealed that the Seminoles, a sovereign nation and a federally recognized tribe, have a deal with the State of Florida, known as the 2021 Gaming Compact. That 30-year contract allows the tribe to maintain what the tribe states is the “exclusive right to offer online sports betting throughout the State of Florida.” In exchange, this betting regime is regulated, and Florida takes a cut.

    But since that contract was signed, attorneys for the Seminole Tribe say in the complaint, DraftKings has pursued years of court challenges and a failed ballot measure designed to break into the Sunshine State.

    As of 2026, DraftKings released “Pick6” in Florida, a game where individuals can put money down while predicting specific outcomes—for example, whether Victor Wembanyama of the San Antonio Spurs will score more or less than 28.5 points in his next basketball game.

    According to recent reports, “Based on DraftKings’ representations, Florida consumers may predictably but incorrectly conclude that Pick6 is a legal product in Florida. It is not,” the complaint states.

    Sources indicate that “Pick6 is illegal ‘gambling’ under Florida law. DraftKings operates Pick6 without a license, without state oversight, and without any consumer protections Florida requires as a condition of legal sports wagering.”.

    In June 2026, DraftKings launched what it calls a “Super App,” which the Seminole Tribe argues is a “one-stop shop for illegal gambling,” as it provides an interface that is “in the same format used by every traditional, regulated sportsbook.”.

    Florida-based professor Robert Jarvis of Nova Southeastern University studies gambling law, and he told Ars by email that he didn’t “buy the argument” DraftKings put forward that its products cannot be regulated under Florida gambling law.

    Jarvis also noted that the tribe caught a break, too, with their randomly assigned federal judge.

    “Not only have they had very good luck in federal court in previous cases, the federal judge assigned to the case is Ed Artau, who previously served as a Florida state trial judge (2014–20) and a Florida state appellate judge (2020–25),” he wrote. “Thus, in a sense, the Seminoles get the best of both worlds: a federal court run by a Florida state judge.”.

According to its official statement, GTA VI's "day one retail sales reached $3.79 billion, setting a upcoming record for entertainment across any medium, and becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.".

    But it's when you put those numbers into perspective that you get a sense of how astonishingly successful Rockstar's launch truly was. Spider-Man: Brand New Day is the highest-grossing movie of 2026, according to Box Office Mojo, with worldwide ticket sales exceeding $2.5 billion. That film was released at the end of July, more than three months ago, but Grand Theft Auto VI has already exceeded its worldwide box office total by more than a billion dollars.

    In a recent development, but what if we widened our search? On Box Office Mojo's ranking of the highest-grossing movies of all time, 2019's Avengers: Endgame ranks near the top with worldwide ticket sales of over $2.9 billion — still well short of Rockstar's GTA VI score.

    Recent findings suggest that rockstar's co-founder and current president Sam Houser was understandably elated by the reception to his firm's magnum opus: "It is with immense gratitude that we enter a fresh chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you.".

    But the good news likely doesn't end there. Rockstar Games and parent manufacturer Take-Two Interactive have at least two more major paydays to look forward to: the release of Grand Theft Auto VI on the multiplayer platform GTA Online and the future PC port, which would give PC players a chance to buy the game.     Exclusive: Independent candidate Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s cards instruct people to vote in a way that would benefit Liberal party.

    Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

    The Victorian Greens are seeking an urgent injunction from the supreme court to stop an independent candidate distributing how-to-vote cards that allegedly mimic the party’s branding and urge people to preference it last.

    As prepoll opened on Wednesday morning, Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign team handed out how-to-vote cards that used the minor party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo with the banner “Vote 1 Green Values”.

    In a recent development, the card instructed people to vote in a way that would ultimately benefit the Liberal party. It asked voters to give their first preference to Finnigan followed by an Animal Justice party candidate, another independent candidate and then the Liberals in fourth place.

    The Greens are determined to win back the ultra-marginal seat it lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection with a 1.3% margin. Labor is running an open ticket in Prahran, which the Greens fear could deprive it of the preference votes it needs.

    On Wednesday afternoon, the Greens state director, Martin Shield, requested Finnigan immediately stop distributing the material and threatened to take legal action if an undertaking was not given to do so in less than two hours.

    Finnigan agreed to the request and produced an amended how-to-vote card within hours that included different colours with a revised banner that said “Vote 1 Trans Greens Values”.

    “Due to legal threats from the Greens party, I confirm that I am not an endorsed Greens party candidate,” a disclaimer on Finnigan’s revised how-to-vote card said.

    Sources indicate that but the changes did not satisfy the Greens. On Friday afternoon, the party’s lawyers lodged papers in the supreme court.

    At an initial hearing on Friday night, the Greens’ lawyer, Adam McBeth, alleged people handing out Finnigan’s material at prepoll wore shirts with the exact shade of green as worn by genuine Greens party volunteers.

    Sources indicate that mcBeth alleged Finnigan’s team stood next to Greens party volunteers and Greens placards. The party argues voters at prepoll were deliberately misled.

    “There is no other reason for an independent candidate who has an infinite range of colours and styles to choose from to so closely mimic the Greens, including the way people paid to hand out were dressed and where they were directed to stand,” McBeth stated.

    Finnigan, who was self-represented, mentioned they had gone above and beyond to promptly make changes to their initial how-to-vote card and accused the Greens of using “legal manoeuvres” to stop them campaigning.

    “It is my belief that they don’t want me to hand out on Saturday, which will be one of the busiest days of prepoll,” Finnigan said.

    It has been revealed that finnigan told the court that they did not have enough money to print newly introduced cards. They remarked their campaign team had not been instructed to stand next to the Greens at prepoll.

    “I am someone who holds Greens values, of course I am going to have some kind of green shirt,” Finnigan said.

    Recent findings suggest that “The honest reason I went for that colour of green is because the colour is called Irish green and I am of Irish background. That’s why I went for it. I just like the sound of Irish green.”.

    On Friday evening, after the supreme court action was lodged, the Victorian Election Commission (VEC) accepted Finnigan’s subsequent how-to-vote card and published it online.

    Justice John Watson said the first how-to-vote card “looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate”, but he adjourned the matter until 3pm on Saturday to hear testimony from the VEC.

    A decision on whether to grant an injunction will be made on Sunday morning.

    According to recent reports, finnigan became Victoria’s first openly transgender councillor in 2023 when they were elected to the Colac Otway shire council after a countback. They resigned from the council in October 2024.

    Sources indicate that the former Labor field campaigner founded the Restore Democracy Sack Dan Andrews party in 2022. They unsuccessfully contested an upper house seat for the party, securing 1% of first preference votes.

    After working in the offices of Labor ministers during the 2014 state campaign, Finnigan became a whistleblower in the so-called Red Shirts scandal, which saw taxpayer funds used to pay electorate officers campaigning for Labor.

    Finnigan’s campaign Facebook page carrying an authorisation message describes them as a “Green Independent” and contains attack ads against the minor party.

    Signs it's time to replace your phone's screen protector

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Should you take a screen protector off if it's broken?
    • On a daily basis, your phone can take a beating.
    • According to recent reports, the right screen protector can be a solid line of defense when it comes to keeping your phone in good condition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Should you take a screen protector off if it's broken? Here's all the key maintenance tips and when it's time for a replacement.

    On a daily basis, your phone can take a beating. It's likely in and out of your pocket or bag, tossed on a table or desk, or getting roughed up by your keys. And because phones aren't cheap, there's a good chance you've got a screen protector, in case your phone jumps out of your hand and onto the concrete.

    According to recent reports, the right screen protector can be a solid line of defense when it comes to keeping your phone in good condition. It can ward off scratches and cracks and cut down on the inevitable wear and tear that comes with carrying around a device everywhere. There are other reasons you might be interested in a screen protector too, beyond damage protection. For example, you might opt for one that reduces glare and blue light, particularly if you use your phone a lot. You can also find screen protectors that make it harder for people around you to see what's on your screen, if you're interested in upping your privacy. Just don't use a screen protector on a foldable screen. It has one applied at the factory and can end up causing problems rather than preventing them.

    According to recent reports, regardless of your reason for selecting a screen protector, you shouldn't keep it on for the duration of your phone's life — especially if you're seeing cracks, discoloration or peeling. Here are some signs it's time to replace it.

    There are a few ways to know if it's time to replace your screen protector. Visible damage is the most obvious indicator. If your screen protector is coming loose, bubbling, peeling or has scratches on it, it could be your moment to get a newly introduced one. There are also other signs to keep an eye out for. For example, your screen protector might start to yellow, or the touch screen might seem less sensitive.

    Recent findings suggest that you might even see a haze develop, or notice that the screen isn't quite as clear. Smudges and fingerprints might not wipe off as easily as they used to, which could be a sign that the oleophobic coating is wearing away. An oleophobic coating is what fends off oil, like what might transfer from your fingers to your screen.

    Part of the reason you'll want to keep an eye out for these signs is that a deteriorating screen protector won't be as effective in safeguarding your phone. There's no set timeline for how long a screen protector will last. It will depend, in part, on how you use it and the quality and makeup of the protector.

    Sources indicate that there are also a few ways you can take care of your screen protector along the way. For one, use a microfiber cloth to clean the protector without damaging it. Avoid anything abrasive like paper towels. It's also a good idea to know what your screen protector might be made of or coated with, whether it's an oleophobic coating or an anti-blue light coating.

    It has been revealed that using certain cleaning agents could actually strip your screen protector's coating. This can include harsh chemicals like ammonia or bleach. Alcohol in a higher concentration could also be a problem. Something like a disinfectant wipe might hurt a coating, even if a wipe seems pretty benign. The FCC also warns against spraying anything directly onto your phone. Instead, use that microfiber cloth. Dampening it will be enough.

    Also know that factors like extreme temperatures, improper installation or excess pressure can all contribute to issues like cracks forming in your screen protector. So, if you're looking to extend the life of both your phone's screen and the protector on it, you can take a few precautions to do just that before the next time your phone takes a swan dive out of your hands.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • United Nations talks on regulating lethal autonomous weapons systems ended on Saturday without an agreement on a legally binding ban.
    • The negotiations did, however, yield an agreement for further discussions to develop latest rules by 2028.
    • Delegates from 128 states that are parties to the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) had been meeting in Geneva since Monday amid rising concerns over the use of the so-called killer robots in global conflicts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    United Nations talks on regulating lethal autonomous weapons systems ended on Saturday without an agreement on a legally binding ban.

    The negotiations did, however, yield an agreement for further discussions to develop latest rules by 2028.

    Delegates from 128 states that are parties to the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) had been meeting in Geneva since Monday amid rising concerns over the use of the so-called killer robots in global conflicts.

    The conference ended early on Saturday in what campaigners deemed a "weakened" outcome, following several hours of overnight parleying.

    Nearly 100 nations had called for negotiations on a legally binding agreement on the systems capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.

    UN Secretary-General António Guterres, Pope Leo XIV and the Red Cross had also supported a ban on killer robots.

    However, countries that have the technology, including arms-producing giants like the ​US, Russia ‌and Israel, were among those opposing the mandate.

    Ultimately, the 128 countries  "agreed to launch the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems, which should be conducted over the next two years", the conference's Swiss chair, Julien Thoni, told the media on Saturday.

    But while Thoni hailed a multilateral diplomacy delivering "concrete results" even in "today's deeply divided world," rights groups expressed disappointment at the minimal agreement.

    "States adopted a watered-down mandate that fails to chart a clear path towards a legally binding instrument," news agency AFP quoted Stop Killer Robots, a global coalition of over 300 organizations, as saying.

    "Over 95 states expressed their support for a treaty. In the final hours, a small number of states weakened the mandate introducing uncertainty about the legal status of the final document," it added.

    The group had earlier said that autonomous weapons systems were already reaching the battlefield and such systems had been tested or deployed, including in the Ukraine war.

Zero, and the executable drops, no conditions. Unless the CYBERLEEK token reaches 15 million market cap first — then it drops immediately.".

    #82075. Breaking: Here's how much a Sony Walkman cost in 1980 vs. 2026

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (633 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Here's how much a Sony Walkman cost in 1980 vs. 2026

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Sony Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player cost a lot more than people think when considering inflation.
    • Sources indicate that sony might not have been the first to release a magnetic cassette player, but it sure made them popular.
    • At the time, it took a while to convince skeptics and consumers to try a 14-ounce tape player without recording capabilities.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Sony Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player cost a lot more than people think when considering inflation.

    Sources indicate that sony might not have been the first to release a magnetic cassette player, but it sure made them popular. Its Walkman players changed how people listened to music. Tapes once reserved for listening at home or in the car could now be strapped to your belt.

    At the time, it took a while to convince skeptics and consumers to try a 14-ounce tape player without recording capabilities. But with the help of street-level marketing, the now-iconic TPS-L2 Walkman (which we've asked readers to review) went on to sell 30,000 units in two months after its 1979 debut in Japan. In 1986, the word "Walkman" even made its way into the Oxford English Dictionary, cementing a portable audio legacy that collectors still hunt down.

    Industry observers note that sony sold over 200 million cassette-based players before it stopped making them in 2010. Originally called Soundabout in the US, the player eventually had its branding standardized to Walkman. Sony would rule over personal audio players for about two decades before MP3 players and the iPod took over. Here's what you'd have paid for one of its most recognizable pieces of hardware back then and how much Sony's newer audio devices cost.

    In a recent development, when the TPS-L2 Walkman celebrated its 40-year anniversary in 2019, its launch price alone put its influence into perspective. When it came to the Western market in 1980, it cost $200. Accounting for inflation, it would be valued at about $800 today. Built with a modified Sony Pressman recorder chassis, the portable stereo cassette player had two mini headphone jacks for two simultaneous listeners.

    It has been revealed that its blue-and-silver metal housing and orange foam earpads on the bundled MDR-3L2 headphones became a familiar sight. A "hotline" button lowered the volume and activated a microphone, letting people speak with someone without taking off their headphones. Two AA batteries kept the music going.

    After decades of being a staple in the audio player space, chatter around Walkman devices faded as Apple iPod and mobile phones took over. In 2014, Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy film brought the TPS-L2 back into the limelight. Protagonist Peter Quill, played by Chris Pratt, used it to play the Awesome Mix Vol. 1 tape, a gift from his mother in the film — driving vintage TPS-L2 prices into the hundreds or thousands of dollars among collectors.

    Targeted at audiophiles, Sony's newer Walkman players cost more than most modern smartphones, even the folding ones. If money is no object, the oddly named $5,900 NW-WM1ZM3 digital audio player (DAP) — roughly $1,500 in 1980 dollars — packs Android, Wi-Fi streaming and a 5.5-inch touchscreen into a precision-milled oxygen-free copper chassis. Sony promises the flagship player delivers "authoritative bass, clarity and dynamic sound.".

    A more reasonable choice for most people is the $350 midrange NW-A306 from 2023, which supports hi-res files and high-quality codecs, albeit at a paltry 32GB of storage (with only about 16GB usable). Budget models like Sony's $75 NW-E394 stick to the basics, losing Android support, Bluetooth and SD card expansion. The latter particularly hurts as its 8GB of internal storage runs out pretty quickly.

    It has been revealed that after the TPS-L2 Walkman, Sony built on its success with the Discman and MiniDisc players before switching over to modern portable media players. The world may have moved on to streaming apps and the brand might not be as recognizable, but the Walkman's DNA lives on in how we approach the intersection of music and technology today. From the original's $200 price tag in 1980 to today's $75 to $5,900 range, the cost of entry has certainly evolved right alongside the hardware.

    Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
