    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration.
    • In a recent development, the nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13.
    • Industry observers note that nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA’s effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved.

    In a recent development, the nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic.

    Industry observers note that nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN. Bedford also stated that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy looks to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20.

    According to recent reports, problems first arose when “data began flooding” the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network with 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, according to an FAA Q&A post on November 15. The FTI network supports the flow of crucial flight data along with voice and video communications to air traffic control centers across the country.

    Industry observers note that that caused “instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds” at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers that manage en-route air traffic across the country, according to the FAA. The instability also impacted several Terminal Radar Approach Control facilities that guide aircraft both on approach and when departing from airports.

    An initial agency investigation identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, as “the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems.” The FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was installing a new router at the El Dorado site when the incident occurred and had recently installed a similar router in Texas.

    Specifically, the L3Harris contractor was deploying a newly introduced Juniper Networks router to replace a 25-year-old Cisco router at the El Dorado site. But the subsequent incident prompted the FAA to pause installation of the Juniper routers and turn off those that had already been installed, falling back on the older Cisco routers, according to the Associated Press.

    FAA employees typically conduct risk assessments and coordinate with contractors, such as L3Harris technicians, on system maintenance or upgrades, according to The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union that represents FAA technicians. But in a statement, the union noted that none of its FAA technicians were involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.

    According to recent reports, similarly, CNN reported that the router replacement at the remote radio communications site in El Dorado was done by an L3Harris engineer without direct FAA oversight. The union and two sources told CNN that the FAA technician merely escorted the contractor into the facility and then turned his attention elsewhere without knowing what work the contractor was doing.

    According to recent reports, to get a former insider perspective, Ars conducted a lengthy interview with Philip Mann, a principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years, starting as a technician at Denver International Airport and eventually becoming a training program manager at the FAA Academy in Oklahoma City.

    (This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.).

    Ars Technica: What do you see as some of the potential contributing factors that led to the nationwide ground stop?

    Philip Mann: I spent a lot of time as a technician, and then did a bunch of things in between. And later on, I was an instructor at the FAA Academy, and then I did training program management. So I’ve seen a lot of this from all sides about how it’s supposed to work, and the thing that stood out to me the most immediately when I saw this is the time during the day in which the work was being done.

    As an FAA technician, this is managed at the field person level. This is not like a top-down command-control thing. It is your job to cultivate a little credulity and think, “Okay, this thing I’m working on, what’s the worst thing that could happen? How far can it reach? What’s the blast radius?” This impacted a nationwide network, so by default the blast radius is the largest possible blast radius, so that basically means you take the maximum possible mitigations.

    To kind of contrast that, when I worked at Denver [International Airport], a lot of times I was working on things that were on a single runway, like one approach lighting system or one electronic system, and the blast radius was just that runway, not even the whole airport, just that specific runway, and sometimes only that one end of that one runway. So you can still use the rest of it just fine.

    Sources indicate that and then maybe we work on a radar site, and a radar site might have a little more of a regional area. Most of the ones I worked on were kind of short-range radar, so it might be like a 50-mile radius or something. In which case you look at what the edges are, and you assume that if something goes wrong, that whole area just goes dark for air traffic controllers.

    Recent findings suggest that so you strategy around that, and the coordination goes on up to regional, national stuff like this. And this is the far end of that, just basic risk management stuff. The bigger the potential impact, the more people and operations potentially affected, the more you emphasize doing things like working at night when there’s less traffic, which is when this should have been done.

    And even Duffy has kind of acknowledged that [the FAA] confused the physical location of the facility with how far that system and service could reach within the national airspace system, and they had it completely backward. Yeah, on a map this is out in the middle of nowhere, but in a network diagram this router was immediately adjacent to all 22 of the [FAA’s air route traffic control] centers. Of those, 17 were affected, but it was immediately adjacent to all 22 of them.

    That was the thing that immediately struck me: How clear it is that basic impact analysis and basic risk management seems to have just been completely gone.

    It even goes a little bit further than that. As a technician, we used to have this rule that you don’t break anything on a Friday. We would actually not schedule certain work past lunch, and it wasn’t to get people off early. It was basically because, if something broke, somebody was going to have to come in on Saturday to fix it. You break it Thursday, people are going to be in on Friday anyway.

    And then we had the commandment: “Thou shalt not be on the front page of the newspaper,” and it seems like all of that was missing here.

    L3Harris should know better, because Harris has a history. Back in 2009, they misconfigured something and caused a big network outage. At the time, they had only identified a small handful—I want to say it was like a couple dozen potential areas of impact—and it wound up being like six times that. So they should know better.

    (Ars note: The 2009 network incident was caused by a Harris technician incorrectly configuring a router that directs air traffic data through the FAA telecommunications network. That error ended up delaying thousands of travelers and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide.).

    I don’t know how it was done on site, but when I did this work, quite often when contractors were working, I was the person who was there that got them cleared to the fence, that got their badges, that got them scheduled, that did the coordination with the airport authorities, and whatever else we had to do.

    Industry observers note that so there was always an FAA person that was the point of contact, and even on some facilities it might have to be an FAA person that physically pushes the button to turn the system back on. Like in a lot of cases, a contractor cannot do that, and it might be quite literally as simple as just flipping a switch. But the thing is, that action puts that system onto the national airspace system. That has to be done by the government. It can’t be done by a contractor.

    According to recent reports, now, I don’t know if that’s the case here. I’m just saying it’s typical.

    Ars Technica: The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union representing FAA technicians put out a statement saying that, “historically contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment.” The union then noted that “PASS-represented technicians” were not involved in the upgrades on the “contractor owned and maintained routers” that led to the ground stop.

    Industry observers note that mann: In my experience, the union a lot of times is one of the groups that raises their hand and claims, “Hey, hold on, we need a qualified person. What does that actually mean? Like, who on this list of people is qualified? Does that mean that they’ve had the class? Does that mean they’ve got a certification? Does that mean they’ve been here for a certain period of time?” But they’ll figure that out, and the answer is not always the same.

    It has been revealed that so, in a different FAA system at a different time, we had to get somebody who had been to a specific set of schools and, in one case, some specific vendor schools. The FAA at that time had only sent like a half-dozen people through those schools because they’re really expensive and really long. They had a couple in the east, a couple in the west, a couple in the middle, and every time they did one of these projects they would grab one of those people and put them on there, because that’s what a qualified person is.

    Maybe they had somebody for the FAA that was there, but maybe that person was a upcoming hire who was administratively qualified to be on site, meaning they had their background check and their driver’s license and had their access badges and all that. But maybe they didn’t even have a networking background or whatever. They were just the person who had the access and the free time and could be there.

    But this is certainly a case, especially with the national-size blast radius of a network, that highlights the importance of having that qualified person, whatever that means. That is very much a union push to make sure that we know what the right qualified person means, that we know how to identify those people and that we’re treating those people fairly.

    Sources indicate that it’s notable to understand that in the union leadership, they’re all former technicians and engineers, everybody who runs that union. Even the local shop people are all fully qualified. So they all know what’s going on. Their role in all this potentially is to cover that blind spot that management and contractors share.

    Ars Technica: Based on what you described, it does sound like both the contractor side and the current FAA side were underestimating the potential blast radius for whatever reason.

    Mann: Well, yeah, and Duffy has even indicated that they mistook the physically remote location for being a network remote location, and those two don’t correspond to each other. Duffy has said that it was the physical smallness and the physical remoteness of the site that somehow let them forget about what they were actually working on.

    Ars Technica: That’s kind of astounding, isn’t it? It’s like the current FAA leadership acknowledging that somehow they didn’t know about their own network and the importance of different nodes in the network.

    Mann: In recent years they’ve brought a lot more people into the fold with the FAA, and you can see that overall a lot of it is more Silicon Valley-type people. It’s not aviation people or risk people or even necessarily physical engineering people. And I make that separate distinction because physical engineering is way more rigorous than anything like software engineering—that’s hopefully public knowledge.

    It has been revealed that but they get a lot of people who’ve got the “move fast, break things” approach that even [Mark] Zuckerberg stopped believing in. They’ve got the “deploy it now, patch it later” mindset, like “Oh well, we just reboot it, or if it goes down, we’ll just be down for a little while; we’ll lose a few ad dollars or whatever.”.

    But the national airspace system is a whole different animal, because the national airspace system has to work all the time.

    Sources indicate that it is possible to bring things down and to do it in a scheduled way. We would shut down radar sites on purpose, but we would also put NOTAMs [Notice to Airmen advisories] out saying, “Hey, this airspace is not covered by radar right now,” and some of that stuff is done weeks and weeks and weeks in advance.

    Now, at a national network scale, there’s not really a way to say, “By the way, just in case we might shut the NAS off, we might shut down all the airspace because we’re not sure if this one little router out in Arkansas someplace is going to cause problems.”.

    In a recent development, I have ideas about how this might have happened, but the long and short of it is, when they plugged it in, they didn’t adequately test it before they connected it back to the network some way somehow, and it could have been misconfigured. Maybe there was an approved configuration, somebody didn’t have it, so they just kind of winged it, or it could be that somebody got the wrong configuration. But again, we’ll wait for the root cause to come out, if it comes out sometime later.

    Ars Technica: What are the main things that should have been done to prevent this from becoming a whole nationwide incident?

    Recent findings suggest that mann: An crucial caveat is, I don’t know if this was a misconfiguration or just somebody making a mistake, or just a bad configuration that shouldn’t have worked. I don’t know how much testing was done.

    It has been revealed that but what should have happened is, with whatever necessary level of technician and engineer engagement, they should have done the blast radius assessment, the risk assessment. Duffy has already conceded they did not do a sufficient risk assessment. He has not mentioned it exactly that way, but he has said that they misunderstood the risk in not so many words. They should have pulled up the network topology and looked at what does this actually touch.

    It has been revealed that one of the systems I used to work on a lot was backup power, so backup generators attached to a radar site. I was working on the generator, but I still marked the radar site as potentially out of service, because the power generator affects the radar site, and if the generator crashes, it’s going to take the radar site down.

    Industry observers note that so in a network, that’s just a million times more complex, because you really need to go, “How far could this reach?” You, of course, want to understand that at the networking level. You want to understand what all that is, but what they need to do is the proper risk assessment.

    Do whatever engineering, whatever tests, whatever scenario things they want to do and really, really, really embrace that it’s not what you’ve seen before. What is the boundary of what is prohibited by physics? You’re talking about an interconnected network. There is nothing in physics that says a data bit from this router can’t get to the far end of the universe if they’re all connected. And thinking about that kind of stuff, assume it might fail.

    Sources indicate that that’s the first massive thing, and that should have taken whatever amount of time it took. Because the benefit with this kind of a system is that same basic impact assessment, you know, plus or minus maybe a couple of relatively small variables, is going to apply to every single one of these installations across the entire country. If they’re doing one of them or doing 1,000 of them, they’re all network-interconnected devices that all do the same thing and all hit the same network.

    Industry observers note that so it sounds bad when you think about doing it for every single site separately, but when you do a full network analysis, you’re like, “We’ve got to do this really hard thing one time, and then we’ve got to assess to see if there’s been any changes as we migrate this network piece by piece.” Does the latest router significantly change anything? But it’s pretty easy from there.

    According to recent reports, then, and this is the important part, then they need to behave as if they’re trying to keep that worst-case scenario thing from happening. Or even if they can’t keep it from happening, reduce the impact as much as possible.

    So do it at midnight when, if you have a complete mass outage like this, it’s not too many travelers. Maybe a couple red-eye flights, a few cargo planes like UPS, FedEx, because those guys fly at night a lot, but it’s not 12,000 passenger planes.

    That may not have prevented the absolute failure whenever we find out what that is, but it would have reduced how bad it got. If you’ve already done that kind of risk assessment, and you’ve briefed everybody accordingly, your technicians are sitting there in the building—hopefully they’re the right people—and they’re already braced to recover.

    Every time I started an engine generator that was going to run a radar site, I would hold my breath for a second when I flipped a switch, because things can happen. You can do everything right, and you flip a switch, and the engine throws a rod or something. Nothing you could do about it. Nothing you would know to prevent or anything like that. But we would hold our breath for a second, make sure everything was operating fine. Go outside, look up, make sure the antenna is still spinning, all that kind of stuff.

    In a recent development, it is the same kind of thing. These technicians, if they’re braced and ready to intercept the early signs of that worst case scenario failure, they’re not casual about it. They’re really thinking, “Okay, we need to watch this and look for any unusual behavior early, and then be ready to shut it back off or pull the plug or whatever if we start seeing something we’re not comfortable with.”.

    You’re kind of chopping off the impact from both sides a little bit. Technicians are more prepared to catch it faster, and even if it goes for a little bit, it’s not going to affect nearly as many people.

    In a recent development, in this case it’s possible—don’t know but it’s possible—if this would have been at 2 or 3 o’clock in the morning, it might have started lighting up some lights somewhere, but they could have potentially shut it down, because you don’t have so many flights and data overloading the network. It’s possible, and just my speculation, it’s possible they could have seen it, flipped it off, let everything calm down, and not had a ground stop at all.

    According to recent reports, ars Technica: The router installation issue that led to the nationwide ground stop was part of an ongoing FAA effort to modernize its overall system. What might this event indicate about the current state of the US National Airspace System?

    It has been revealed that mann: This is one of the challenges with the FAA modernization. When they do that properly, nobody sees that there’s that kind of danger out there. It’s kind of the paradox of risk analysis, right? The better you are at it, the less essential people think it is, and that’s the FAA being a victim of its own success for the last 50 years. I’m not in that camp that everything that sounds old needs to be replaced. Floppy disks are totally fine as long as they still work, I don’t care.

    But the agency has had a hard time modernizing, in part, I believe, because it is so safe and its risk management is normally so good that people lose sight of the fact that there isn’t modernization that needs to be done.

    It’s not that they don’t want to modernize, and it’s not like the FAA doesn’t want to modernize. It’s just that it’s the old squeaky wheel thing, right? The FAA is so good at what it does that when it comes time to write checks, there’s always a different squeaky wheel that needs the money more.

    Sources indicate that actually, I’m kind of happy for the current administration keeping this at the front. I don’t necessarily like how they’re doing it, but I do like that they’re making this a live concern in Congress. They’re making this a live issue even out here in different airports. I’ll talk to people and they’re like, “Hey, when are we going to modernize this?” Ten years ago, not too many people out in the public were talking about it.

    I think the NAS is still just as safe as it’s always been. We can kind of be grateful. Folks probably ought to understand that because they see this on the news, it means it’s weird. It’s unusual. But it’s good that we can be safe and we can still have the conversation about it, about what needs to happen to keep it safe, because we don’t want to have a catastrophic failure somewhere down the line that really is because something failed or really is because something was neglected, and then try to say, “Oh yeah, now we’ve got to shut down our airspace for six months because something happened.”.

    I’m not a blank check person. I do not want [Congress] just writing a check and handing it to Duffy or anybody. I want them to do the proper acquisition oversight, do the proper union involvement, do the proper technical evaluations, all that kind of stuff, because that is money well spent.

    Industry observers note that we could have been really unlucky. We could have lost communication to all the aircraft that were in the air entirely. We could have lost the ability to be able to manage those aircraft, and then we would have been back to doing 1950s, 1960s kind of stuff, like call the airplane and have the airplane tell us where it is. And we probably would have seen some bad outcomes from that.

    Ars Technica: It is definitely sobering to think that this was in some ways the best-case scenario from the situation that unfolded.

    Sources indicate that mann: This was a best and worst [case]. In the resilience of the system, this was a best case because the system degraded all the way down to its essential mission of just keeping the aircraft safe. And an aircraft parked on the ground is as safe as it’s ever going to be, and the system was successful. The system is very resilient. It decayed down to its essential mission, and preserved that essential mission at the expense of literally everything else.

    It has been revealed that the apparent lack of risk analysis is a very clear example of the worst case scenario. The network-spanning maintenance being done in the middle of the day and allowed to cascade as a failure into the entire NAS, that was horrible. So a single set of technologies failed, but the NAS itself indicated its resilience in preserving that key mission all the way down to the minimum function, to the absolute zero, where the only piece left was just keep it safe. That’s what it’s supposed to do.

    In a recent development, we don’t want to see it go that far down. We’d much rather have them just divert flights a couple minutes here and there. But if we need to get it all the way down to the only thing we have is safe aircraft, I’m good with that.

    Ars Technica: Duffy is saying the FAA needs $50 billion to make sure this doesn’t happen again. And if I understood correctly, you were saying it is good to have support for enough funding for the FAA to do what it needs to do, even if Duffy tying it specifically to “this happened because we didn’t have enough money” is not necessarily the correct assessment.

    Recent findings suggest that mann: Yeah. This happened because there wasn’t the right oversight. I’d be pretty confident to say that. If we just take $50 billion and throw it at the same people doing the same thing the same way, we don’t get a better system. We just get a whole bunch more of this.

    It has been revealed that because hiring more contractors and getting more routers replaced faster in the middle of the day with no risk assessment and incorrect configurations or however it came about… take some of that money and put it into oversight, put it into testing, and put it into whatever you need to do to make sure that however many more of these we’re going to do are done properly, and in this case, at 2 o’clock in the morning with a team of qualified people with the proper testing, people ready to pull a plug on it, all that kind of stuff. That’s money well spent.

    It has been revealed that ars Technica: Many people have noted the coincidence of the FAA’s SMART AI system being deployed nationwide in the same week as the router issue that led to the ground stop. The FAA has remarked the SMART rollout had no connection to what ensued. What is your view on all this?

    In a recent development, mann: I get that. I think it is a coincidence. This particular router was just one of a long series of these replacements being done—they don’t take 1,000 routers and just replace them all on a Thursday. They might do one or two of them a night for a couple of years.

    Now, just to lean into it a little bit, it could be totally possible that the router’s capabilities, or maybe something that was configured or misconfigured, is a facilitating technology for SMART. In other words, it’s not intended to be used right now, but they’re putting in a placeholder.

    If you’ve got a deployment, you’ve got three steps. You’ve got an A, B, C step. Well, if you need some ridiculously high-powered, super fast switch or something at step C, you might put that in at step A, knowing you’re not using its full capability, because that’s when it makes sense to do that. Maybe it’s difficult infrastructure, physically hard to do or whatever.

    But you put the super-fast switch in it at A, then you do step B, then you do step C, and only at that time when you get to step C are you actually going to start using the capabilities in that switch. And those might be years apart. I can imagine something like that being a subtext.

    Industry observers note that but the thing is, the SMART system looks out weeks and months in the future. It doesn’t touch the operation. It reads data, it does some stuff and makes some advising comments and makes some advising predictions, and then tells the air traffic control center folks, “Hey, y’all might want to do this.”.

    It has been revealed that to the best of my knowledge and in my opinion, the SMART system doesn’t touch the actual operational data. In other words, it’s not something that reaches out across the whole network. It has certain data sets that are at the control center or wherever it is. There’s certain data that it has access to that it cannot push information into. It just draws from data and does analysis, and then it provides a recommendation to the traffic managers, and then those traffic managers act or don’t act on that information in some way.

    SMART is a system that reads. You can think of it as a Wall Street guy who reads the ticker and makes some calculations and then hands a spreadsheet to the trader. The analyst is not the trader. The analyst is literally reading the screen, running some math, and then handing a ticket to the trader, and a trader makes the final decision.

    That’s kind of what happens where the system looks at what’s going on in NAS, what’s forecast to go on in NAS, weather, all that kind of stuff, and then it does some calculations and it effectively hands a slip of paper to the air traffic controllers and says, “Hey, you might want to do this.” But none of that would mean that it’s Skynet getting onto the network or something like that.

    This story was updated on November 20, 2026 to correct the description of the FAA ground stop’s impact on aircraft arrivals and departures. It was also updated to clarify one of Mann’s comments on the “move fast, break things” approach.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of consumers — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.
    • The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of consumers — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.

    The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”.

    The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”.

    TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.

    Sources indicate that agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have debuted such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.

    Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.

    The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging customers from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the tech giant planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

    Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”.

    #82046. The trade-offs of using Apple's AirPods Max headphones

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (739 w)

    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    The trade-offs of using Apple's AirPods Max headphones

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Apple's AirPods Max sound great, but they come with a lot of compromises for $549 headphones.
    • Recent findings suggest that there's a lot to love about the AirPods Max, Apple's premium headphones that recently got a nice revision with improved ANC and the H2 chip.
    • According to recent reports, the AirPods Max are quite heavy compared to their main competitors, and that might bother some people.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Apple's AirPods Max sound great, but they come with a lot of compromises for $549 headphones.

    Recent findings suggest that there's a lot to love about the AirPods Max, Apple's premium headphones that recently got a nice revision with improved ANC and the H2 chip. For iPhone people, they definitely play nicely with the Apple ecosystem thanks to features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness and Live Translation, not to mention that the audio quality is really good. But the AirPods Max aren't perfect. At $549, they're too expensive for headphones that haven't changed much since 2020. They're also heavy and come with a clunky case. If you've been thinking about buying the AirPods Max, there are a few trade-offs you definitely need to consider before making your decision.

    According to recent reports, the AirPods Max are quite heavy compared to their main competitors, and that might bother some people. It's true that they have a super-premium design made of aluminum and steel, but all that adds up to 386 grams (13.6 ounces). By comparison, the mostly plastic Beats 360 weigh only 294 grams (10.4 ounces) and definitely feel lighter when you wear them for more than an hour. Wearing the AirPods Max for long periods of time, like during a long flight, can really make you aware of that extra bulk.

    It has been revealed that although they're made with premium materials, the AirPods Max's design is also a bit clunky, especially when it comes to the Smart Case. There's no power button on the AirPods Max. Instead, they rely on the Smart Case to enter sleep mode — which has magnets to tell the headphones that they're stored away and not in use. The thing is, Apple's Smart Case doesn't really protect the AirPods Max. The headband stays exposed and it can easily be damaged if you throw your headphones into a backpack with anything sharp. The ear cups aren't fully protected either. The headphones also don't fold up (only the ear cups rotate flat), so they take up a lot of space in a bag.

    There are many complaints about the AirPods Max headband peeling over time — and since the AirPods Max 2 have exactly the same design as the first generation, it's very unlikely that anything has changed here. There are third-party cases for the AirPods Max that include the magnets needed to put the headphones into sleep mode, but you'll have to spend a few extra dollars on top of the $549 price to fix a design flaw.

    Another major complaint about the AirPods Max is condensation inside the ear cups. A lawsuit filed in 2025 claimed that this moisture could degrade sound quality and cause the ear detection feature to malfunction over time, although a judge later dismissed the case. This problem persists with the AirPods Max 2, and iFixit says there are no visible changes to the internal seals — although Apple claims that the moisture is easy to spot and clean since the ear cups are easily removable. Still, it's something to keep in mind.

    Repairing the AirPods Max is also very difficult. It's not impossible, unlike the smaller AirPods, but taking the headphones apart requires specialized tools and removing a lot of adhesive strips. Apple charges $79 for battery replacements, and that's the only repair the company offers. If any other hardware component fails, Apple replaces the headphones with a latest pair, and that service typically costs around $300. For that price, you can buy a good pair of new headphones — like the new Beats 360, which compare to the AirPods Max in many ways. You are able to replace the ear pads yourself as needed, since these snap on and off easily. A pair of those will cost you $69, unless you opt for a third-party option.

    Recent findings suggest that for audiophiles, the AirPods Max also seem to fall a little short. It's not that they sound bad — they actually sound great. But they still lack codecs for high-res audio over Bluetooth, so you'll need a USB-C cable to get lossless audio. Many other premium headphones on the market already support codecs such as LDAC and aptX HD for higher audio quality over Bluetooth.

    When you put it all in perspective, the AirPods Max seem way too expensive for what they offer. It's a good product, but it's not exceptional for $549.

    Anthropic researcher uses AI to solve math's greatest riddle

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (467 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic indicates he used the organization's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.
    • The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.
    • Levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic indicates he used the organization's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.

    The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.

    Levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," Levent Alpoge wrote in a note released Friday.

    Recent findings suggest that the proof still has to be verified and confirmed by other mathematicians. If it withstands independent examination, it would be a major milestone both in mathematics and the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research.

    The Riemann hypothesis is the latest and most crucial in a string of famous mathematical problems that were tackled with the help of AI.

    Alpoge said that the collaboration with AI had generated more than 250,000 pages of mathematical material, adding that he had not yet mastered all the mathematics involved.

    Sources indicate that "Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," he wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.".

    The Riemann Hypothesis is one of seven major mathematical problems, the so-called Millennium Prize Problems, selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1 million for a solution to each of those.

    "This is an announcement of historic significance," Martin Bridson, president of the institute, said in a statement quoted by news agency AP.

    He added it "holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics.".

    "But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult.".

    Formulated by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in the 19th century, the hypothesis is about the distribution of prime numbers, which are numbers that can only be divided by themselves and the number 1.

    According to recent reports, the hypothesis describes a fundamental pattern of how these numbers are distributed as they become ever larger. Confirming that hypothesis is thought to have crucial implications for a wide range of further mathematical research.

    The potential breakthrough by Alpoge and Claude AI comes amid a growing number of examples where artificial intelligence systems are making significant contributions to advanced mathematical research.

    In September, rival AI manufacturer OpenAI stated its technology had helped solve a problem involving the Navier-Stokes equations.

    The equations, which describe the movement of fluids such as water and air, are another of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, but the claim that they've been solved also still needs independent verification.

    • Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Watch: Inside court as Nikhil Gupta sentenced to 19 years over assassination plot.

    A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.

    Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.

    US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.

    It has been revealed that india has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.

    Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019.

    He previously told the BBC that "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".

    In a recent development, india has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.

    Recent findings suggest that nikhil Gupta (seen in a 2024 courtroom sketch) pleaded guilty in a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a U.S. resident who advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.

    Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.

    Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in Fresh York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors mentioned.

    At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors stated. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.

    Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in Fresh York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.

    "He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.

    Following Gupta's arrest, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs stated that Yadav is no longer employed, external by the Indian government.

    The country also set up an inquiry committee to address security concerns raised by the US, the spokesperson stated.

    Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.

    Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".

    "It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed.".

    Indian man admits plot to kill US-based Sikh separatist leader.

    Recent findings suggest that india crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.

    Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.

    In a victim impact statement to the court, Pannun mentioned the foiled assassination attempt has not deterred his activism.

    "I am entirely willing to take India's bullets if that is the price required to achieve freedom," he wrote.

    Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.

    In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau noted there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.

    Sources indicate that nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.

    The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets.".

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A government in office for more than two years is finally forced to take responsibility and seemingly no longer able to blame its Labor predecessors.
    • Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.
    • At the beginning of another Queensland parliamentary sitting week, anonymous sources were out in force, this time background briefing against the state’s Labor leader, Steven Miles.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A government in office for more than two years is finally forced to take responsibility and seemingly no longer able to blame its Labor predecessors.

    Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

    At the beginning of another Queensland parliamentary sitting week, anonymous sources were out in force, this time background briefing against the state’s Labor leader, Steven Miles.

    It is no great revelation to observers of Queensland politics that Miles, still seemingly bruised from his election loss two years ago, has struggled to find his feet as opposition leader. Many wondered why he wanted to stay on after the party’s drubbing in 2024. Some of Labor’s factional whisperers were telling anyone who would listen that the former premier’s leadership would come to an end in the weeks before Christmas.

    Sources indicate that however, the week in parliament has ended with a revitalised opposition and a wounded LNP government. A government that has for so long seemed untouchable. A government that has now been left battling the perception that it is overseeing a broken health system.

    And a government – now in office for more than two years – finally forced to take responsibility for systems it had promised to repair; seemingly no longer able to legitimately blame the former Labor government for the litany of mistakes that led to the deaths of seven people in the care of Queensland’s health system.

    In a recent development, by the end of the week, parliament heard six people had died waiting for an ambulance in the last three weeks. One man had waited seven hours, another three. All were triaged as urgently in need of attention.

    Another man had taken his own life in the emergency department of the Prince Charles hospital after self-admitting for mental health treatment. It took staff three hours to find him.

    The health minister, Tim Nicholls, is a professional, a 20-year veteran, with the bearing of a well-paid barrister, who led the LNP to an election in 2017.

    But he struggled to cope with the parliamentary barrage.

    In response to a question from Labor’s Joe Kelly, a former nurse, about how many ambulances had been ramped on 3 November, the night a man died while waiting for one in Townsville, Nicholls first criticised the question’s “pettiness”.

    Sources indicate that “What next? Are they going to ask me what the level of fuel was in the back of the ambulances?” he responded.

    “There was no ramping overnight at the Townsville University hospital that night,” he finished.

    “I am very pleased to be able to correct the record for the purposes of the house,” he mentioned, two questions later.

    Recent findings suggest that “There were at that time four ambulances, as I understand it, on the ramp waiting to off-load. That was the situation there.”.

    Nicholls threw the blame at the federal government, at the former Labor state government and its “decade of decline”, a phrase repeated endlessly by government MPs, at overwhelmed hospitals full of “forgotten Australians”, a term used to refer to retirees warehoused in public hospitals for lack of a federally funded retirement home to put them in.

    Endlessly, Labor hounded him: would he meet the families of the dead?

    The answer was not quite no, but never yes either.

    For a government built on a small-target strategy based on responding to the grief of victims of crime – predicated on the fact that any indecisive response to a tragedy would be an inherently unconvincing one – this was a completely different emotional battle.

    By Wednesday, Nicholls was attending an emergency meeting with the premier, David Crisafulli, the health department director general, David Rosengren, and the ambulance service commissioner, Craig Emery.

    The next day, after another bruising question time, he called a press conference.

    Bearing his well-worn years-old folder labelled “LABOR’S HOSPITAL FAILURES”, he insisted that he was taking responsibility – for making sure his subordinates were doing their jobs.

    “I think people would expect that, as the minister, I hold the DG and the commissioner responsible for the services that they deliver, and I seek answers to questions,” he noted.

    “So I sought advice from the commissioner about the steps that they were taking, what was being done to address the need, what was the root cause of the problem.”.

    Nicholls noted the community could have confidence in the triple-zero system and paramedics, promising to reinvest whatever it was he needed to, on advice from his department.

    “Like all Queenslanders, I do have questions regarding the delivery of services because one death that’s unexpected in the community is one too many,” he said.

    “Every available vehicle is on the road. But the glitch is there are simply not enough beds.”.

    After 10 minutes, with many more questions unasked, he abruptly walked off, looking more like a traditional Queensland health minister than any in the LNP cabinet have this term.

    Then Miles stepped up to the microphone. After days of leadership speculation in newspapers – which has been deliberately and mischievously fanned by the government – the former health minister was on much more solid ground.

    “I have never before seen so many preventable deaths of Queenslanders left waiting hours for an ambulance to arrive, only to die before it does,” Miles mentioned.

    “Six, seven, maybe more preventable deaths.

    “It is only getting worse and worse. The worst that it’s ever been.”.

    Recent findings suggest that miles retains significant goodwill from most Labor MPs, but the polls have become hard for most to ignore. Some think he’s simply failed to land enough punches. Others that he hasn’t thrown nearly enough.

    It remains to be seen whether Miles’s decision to come out swinging was the act of an opposition leader with nothing to lose, deciding to fight at five minutes to midnight in his political career.

    One thing is certain. After two years in which the opposition has rarely felt relevant, this week Queensland politics finally felt like a fair fight.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that when the Steam Machine first started shipping in June, Valve remarked it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn’t secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve notes those supply and cost concerns will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change.

    It has been revealed that “We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday. “As a result we don’t yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we’ll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.”.

    In a recent development, if Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025, with additional price hikes happening this year.

    For the Steam Machine, though, Valve may be more susceptible to supply-related price shocks than its larger competitors in the gaming hardware space. Valve “likely [doesn’t] have the same kind of priority as a Nintendo, Sony, or Microsoft when it comes to suppliers,” F-Squared analyst Michael Futter told us earlier this year. And while the bigger players can still negotiate somewhat with chip suppliers, Valve’s Steam Machine is “a niche product that cannot benefit in the same way when it comes to procurement,” Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad mentioned.

    In a recent development, while Valve has not publicly discussed total Steam Machine sales, estimates based on public Steam Top Sellers charts suggest the company was selling 12,000 to 15,000 a week back in July. By contrast, the PS5 has averaged over 300,000 weekly unit sales worldwide in its roughly six years on the market.

    For now, at least, Valve notes it has fulfilled an expectation it set in July that “everyone in the reservation queue will have the option to purchase by the end of this year.” The firm now says there is “no waitlist remaining” for the 512GB Steam Machine model and that “purchase invites” have been sent to the remaining randomized 2TB reservation holders (who placed orders back in April). The 512GB model was even briefly back in stock on the Steam Store yesterday, even as Valve continues to pare down the waitlist for 2TB stock.

    Valve says it aims to release additional updates on Steam Machine availability in January.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The 4th-gen Apple TV 4K comes with a newly introduced remote. Here's what you need to know about it.

    Earlier this October, Apple unveiled its latest Apple TV 4K streaming box. Like most product launches in recent months, the release centered around a "supercharged" AI offering, which Apple believes will transform "how users search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV demonstrates through a full-screen Siri AI experience." In its announcement, Apple touted the AI-enabled fourth generation of its popular streaming hub as the "most immersive home theater experience yet.".

    In a recent development, one of the most underrated aspects of the fresh Apple TV 4K is the introduction of its new remote. At first glance, the Siri Remote doesn't appear much different. Sporting the same sleek silver and black design fashioned with 100 percent recycled aluminum, it retains the touch-enabled clickpad and voice recognition from its previous version. Like its third-generation predecessor, the new Siri Remote uses a USB-C port for quick recharging and better cross-compatibility.

    However, the newly introduced Siri Remote builds on top of this beloved design by adding a more precise Find My feature. With Precision Finding, you can use your phone's Find My app to find exactly where your fourth-gen Siri Remote is hiding. The remote also adds the ability to play a sound when trying to locate it, much to the joy of those affected by the couch-swallowing gremlins plaguing America's living rooms.

    The new Apple TV 4K is now on available for purchase, and the new Siri Remote comes in the box. However, you will also be able purchase the fourth-generation Siri Remote separately via Apple's website or at your local Apple Store.

    Retailing for $59, the remote is compatible with all four generations of the Apple TV 4K, as well as the Apple TV HD. Those holding onto Apple TV models from before 2015 will need to continue digging through their couch cushions.

    In a recent development, this expanded compatibility is notable given Apple's plans for Siri AI. As it stands, the fine print of Apple's press release notes that the newly introduced AI suite isn't exclusive to the new streaming box. Instead, the tech giant is also pushing its Siri AI features to both Apple TV 4K's second- and third-generation boxes. So while you might be tempted to upgrade your streaming box in order to benefit from the faster speeds, an Ethernet port and a built-in microphones, you may also find that upgrading your Apple TV 4K simply isn't worth the $299 price tag. As such, you may want to consider simply upgrade your remote separately and save $240.

    It has been revealed that there is a catch, however. In addition to a compatible streaming device, your fourth-gen Siri Remote will need to be paired with a relatively new iPhone to unlock its Precision Finding feature. As it stands, the feature is available to Apple viewers with an iPhone Duo, iPhone Air, or iPhone 17 or later, except the iPhone 17e. You will also need to run Apple's latest iOS software, iOS 27.

    In a recent development, similar to consumers with a second- or third-generation Siri Remote, those with an older iPhone will be able to use Apple's Find My feature without Precision Finding. This may be a surprise, as Apple's iPhone 15 and 16 models support Precision Finding for products like the AirTag 2. However, some speculate that this is because Apple's Find My tech has transitioned from using its Ultra Wideband chip to Bluetooth 6 technology in this instance.

    Apple promises that its Siri AI will make your Apple TV 4K more helpful and intuitive by adding a "profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions.".

    Recent findings suggest that siri AI allows you to ask your television questions like, "Siri, who won Best Comedy at this year's Emmy Awards?" You can also ask Siri questions about the film or show you are watching, such as filming locations, why recognize a particular actor or whether a movie is appropriate for your children. Responses are overlaid at the corner of your screen in order to not disrupt your viewing experience.

    According to recent reports, in service of this mission, the box has three far-field microphones, extending your hands-free viewing experience across the room. Moreover, advanced echo cancellation allows your Apple TV 4K to isolate your voice and block out the noise, ensuring you don't spend half the show unsuccessfully screaming at Siri. This also means you don't have to speak all of your queries into the Siri Remote; the box itself can hear you.

    In a recent development, the fresh Apple TV 4K also promises significant speed gains. By adding a new A19 chip, Apple claims that its latest streaming box will achieve 50 percent faster CPU performance and up to twice the GPU speeds when compared to its third-gen predecessor. Its AV1 decoder will enable more bandwidth-efficient streams, increasing visual quality without overloading your network.

    Sources indicate that connected to a four compatible HomePods, you can achieve Apple's best surround sound experience. Moreover, you can manage smart home hub notifications with AI-generated camera activity descriptions, doorbell notifications and enhanced control of select accessories.

The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown.

    Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

    Cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director.

    We’ve reached out to the White House for comment.

    #82034. How to easily factory reset your Fitbit

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (705 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    How to easily factory reset your Fitbit

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It can help fix a serious issue or prep your wearable for a new owner.
    • If your Fitbit is acting up, you'll want to restart it, but this is a very different process from a factory reset.
    • There are only a few times you'll want to factory reset a Fitbit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It can help fix a serious issue or prep your wearable for a new owner.

    If your Fitbit is acting up, you'll want to restart it, but this is a very different process from a factory reset. You may want to restart your Fitbit if it won't sync with the Google Health app or isn't registering data. However, if the screen is unresponsive to taps or swipes, or it's frozen on a specific screen, you can force a hard restart, which typically involves pressing and holding a button (or buttons) for a specific period of time until the screen resets. How to restart your Fitbit device varies by model. It's a refresh, like turning something off and on again. A factory reset, on the other hand, removes all unsynced settings and data from the device and brings the wearable back to its original state when it was first purchased.

    There are only a few times you'll want to factory reset a Fitbit. Do this if you're giving it to someone else or selling it. It's also worth doing for data privacy, if the device is no longer functioning properly and you're dropping it off for safe recycling. Finally, it's a last-ditch effort if a restart isn't fixing a major glitch. Factory resetting your Fitbit is simple, but use this option only when necessary.

    Industry observers note that for Fitbits with a screen, go to Settings > About > Device Info > Clear User Data or Factory Reset. You may need to hold down a button on the screen to confirm, and you should feel a slight vibration when it's done and the Fitbit logo reappears on-screen. With the newest Fitbit Edge, it's even easier: swipe down from the top of the screen and select Settings > Clear User Data.

    With older Fitbit trackers, you may have to connect the device to its charger and hold down a button or use a paperclip. With the Fitbit Flex, for example, which does not have a screen, connect the sensor to its charger, plug the charger into your computer via USB, find the black reset hole, and press it for three seconds with a paperclip. Wait for it to light up and confirm the reset.

    Interestingly, the fresh screenless Fitbit Air (see our Fitbit Air review) does not have a traditional factory reset option. Instead, place it on its charger and press and hold the back button for 10 seconds (or until the status light flashes white). This will restart the device. If a new user pairs with the wearable, your account data will be cleared automatically.

    It's a good idea to manually unpair a Fitbit Air from your account first if you're handing it off. In the app, select the device from the top-left corner and, under System, select Disconnect & reset device. If it's not connecting to a new phone, forget it from your phone's Bluetooth menu (Settings > Bluetooth > tap the "i" beside the device and select Forget This Device.

    According to recent reports, A factory reset is a last-resort option. I recently had challenges syncing my Fitbit Edge with my iPhone; it got stuck in a boot loop and froze on a specific screen. Nothing I tried worked until I tried a factory reset.

    Recent findings suggest that it's important to reiterate that a factory reset will erase all data that is stored locally on the device. This could include morning alarms, goals, notification settings, and any unsynced activities. It does not, however, delete data that's already been synced to the Google Health app. After resetting my Fitbit Edge, for example, all my daily data, including steps, workouts, and more, were still accessible in the app.

    Industry observers note that if you're holding onto an older, discontinued Fitbit model and it's still working, look for instructions on how to factory reset it in the supporting documentation online, or check the Help menu in the Google Health app. Whichever model you have, once the factory reset process is done, it's like a new device again, and you can start the pairing and syncing process from scratch. Be patient: It may take some time to start accurately tracking your data again.

    Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1389 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, in a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army declared Thursday that it would delay a strategy to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air.
    • The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs).
    • “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle mentioned in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, in a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army declared Thursday that it would delay a strategy to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted aims later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

    The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

    “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle mentioned in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”.

    Industry observers note that telle claimed that the Army could not delay the detonation any further than Monday due to the state of deterioration of the compound, which is extremely explosive and sensitive. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”.

    According to recent reports, lead azide is a compound used in detonators for munitions and is stockpiled by the US military. In March, the US Army identified that the stockpile in the Iowa facility—the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP)—had deteriorated. The lead azide in the 68 barrels, reported to total around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons), is suspended in a mixture of water and ethanol within the ECMs, but has degraded and crystallized over time. Temperature fluctuations can cause lead azide to dissolve into the water/alcohol solution and recrystallize into needles or platelets, the Army mentioned. In crystallized forms, lead azide becomes extremely sensitive to any physical shock, friction, or heat. The Army determined the current state is a “catastrophically hazardous condition.”.

    In a recent development, in an environmental assessment released Wednesday, the Army said that trying to move the lead azide from its current position for any reason was ruled out. Any sloshing or physical shock from loading, transporting, or burying the barrels for safer detonation would create “an unacceptable safety risk and a high probability of accidental, uncontrolled detonation.”.

    The military considered neutralizing the lead azide using a chemical reagent, but again ruled it out because it remarked the process would require handling the lead azide over an extended period, with barrels neutralized at a rate of 3 to 10 per day. “The chemical neutralization process requires significantly more ‘hands-on’ time and physical manipulation of the drums by personnel over a prolonged 7- to 22-day period, drastically increasing the probability of accidental, fatal detonation during handling,” the Army wrote in its assessment.

    In all, the Army considered a controlled, mitigated “Blow-in-Place” strategy the best option, and it specifically planned for a fall detonation. The Army mentioned the fall weather would “take advantage of periods of reduced thermal cycling and to ensure the lowest impact to facility operations and local agriculture (harvesting).”.

    According to an emergency permit for the detonation from the Environmental Protection Agency, the plan is to place explosive charges and an accelerant on or near each of the ECMs.

    In a recent development, the Army intends to try to mitigate the detonation’s impact with a few simple methods. Those include lime-fill and sand-fill barriers around the ECMs, water cannons and misters to control lead dust in the wake of the explosion, and timing the detonation with ideal weather conditions—avoiding high winds that could increase the area exposed to the plume or, conversely, a thermal inversion that could trap the plume in one place.

    Sources indicate that modeling released Wednesday—based on the conditions for the scheduled detonation on Friday—suggested the plume could deposit lead dust at an amount between 5 and 100 micrograms per square foot in a stretch up to 25 miles north, nearly to Wapello, Iowa. Those levels are above those considered hazardous for floors and windows, respectively. Meanwhile, airborne lead, at a level of 0.18 micrograms per cubic meter, would reach nearly 100 miles north, toward Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The EPA standard for lead levels in the air is 0.15 micrograms per cubic meter.

    Industry observers note that during the detonation, the Army advised residents in the immediate area to consider leaving or at least staying indoors with windows closed. It also recommended people wash their cars if they park outside. Similarly, local fire departments reportedly planned to hose down children’s playgrounds to remove any coating of lead dust in the aftermath, and schools planned closures.

    The Army’s plan was to communicate clearly with the public about the aims, including holding an open-house event on October 15. But while Middletown residents may have been aware of the detonations, Iowans in the projected path of the plume were surprised by the news this week.

    In its environmental risk assessment, the Army noted it planned to mitigate the lead fallout with “rapid excavation” of soil and dust and treat it with a “stabilization agent.” This was to prevent it from remaining in the environment of the military facility, from which it could drift or make its way into groundwater. But the efforts would not mitigate the airborne plume, and lead does not break down in the environment. Children and pregnant people are particularly vulnerable to the neurotoxic effects.

    Amid health and environmental fears, state leaders and residents raised a range of questions Wednesday and Thursday, from how the lead azide was allowed to deteriorate to its current hazardous condition and whether the Army had truly exhausted safer options—options that wouldn’t launch a toxic cloud over a swath of the state.

    Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, wrote on social media that an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”.

    Political leaders in nearby Illinois also chimed in, sending a letter to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, expressing “grave concerns” over the initiative.

    “Alongside our neighbors in Iowa, we are also demanding answers about how this could affect our people’s health and safety,” Illinois Governor JB Pritzker wrote on social media.

    Industry observers note that on Thursday, prior to the announcement of a delay, environmental groups filed a lawsuit seeking a court-ordered pause of the detonation. The groups alleged, in part, that the EPA approved the strategy “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead; and inadequate public notice of the plan to open-detonate hazardous waste due to the extraordinarily rushed timeline set by the Army.” Late Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an emergency stay of the Army’s EPA permit for the demolition, halting prepares until it can review the case.

    Friday morning, the Army, Department of Health and Human Services, and EPA released a joint statement saying:.

    It has been revealed that the entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible. Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized. The entire Trump administration will continue to engage with state and local officials, as well as the broader community, to keep all apprised of updates as they arise.

    Notably, in June, Zeldin listed the EPA’s work with Iowa’s lead azide as one of the top “100 environmental victories that showcase EPA’s unwavering dedication to protecting American families.” The work was number 60 on the list, described as providing “critical emergency support to Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, deploying technical experts for 68 deteriorating drums of explosive lead azide.”.

    This post was updated November 20 to include that the federal appeals court granted a stay in the case brought by the environmental groups.
